$ crop          <chr> "barley", "Peas", "barley", "canola", "Peas", "Spring wh…
$ weight_tonnes <dbl> 44.0, 44.8, 38.0, 34.7, 42.2, -12.4, 29.5, 48.1, 39.2, 4…
$ moisture_pct  <dbl> 10.400, 7.500, 10.200, 7.000, 9.000, 9.700, 9.300, NA, 8…
$ grade         <dbl> 3, 3, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3, 3, 2, 3, 2, 2, 2, 2, 1, 2, 3, 2, 2,…



If the suffix indicated a different unit, removing it would give the wrong answer. Convert the value to the common unit before discarding the label.


8.2.2.3 Duplicates
An exact duplicate repeats the entire row. duplicated() finds the later copy, while distinct() keeps one copy of every unique row:


# Show exact duplicates
deliveries |>
  get_dupes()

nrow(deliveries)

# Keep one copy of each unique row
deliveries <- deliveries |> distinct()
nrow(deliveries)

> # Show exact duplicates
> deliveries |>
+   get_dupes()
No variable names specified - using all columns.
# A tibble: 2 × 7
  ticket_id delivery_date crop  weight_tonnes moisture_pct grade dupe_count
  <chr>     <chr>         <chr>         <dbl>        <dbl> <dbl>      <int>
1 T0012     2025-09-24    Peas           28.9          7.8     2          2
2 T0012     2025-09-24    Peas           28.9          7.8     2          2
> 
> nrow(deliveries)
[1] 62
> 
> # Keep one copy of each unique row
> deliveries <- deliveries |> distinct()
> nrow(deliveries)
[1] 61



A conflicting duplicate repeats an identifier but not the whole row. Ticket T0030 appears with two different weights, so distinct() keeps both. Count the identifier to find it:


# Find and inspect repeated ticket numbers
deliveries |>
  get_dupes(ticket_id)

> # Find and inspect repeated ticket numbers
> deliveries |>
+   get_dupes(ticket_id)
# A tibble: 2 × 7
  ticket_id dupe_count delivery_date crop   weight_tonnes moisture_pct grade
  <chr>          <int> <chr>         <chr>          <dbl>        <dbl> <dbl>
1 T0030              2 2025-10-23    Barley          38.8          9.6     1
2 T0030              2 2025-10-23    Barley          43            9.6     1



The data alone does not say which row is correct. Check the source record. If that is impossible, report how the conflict was handled.


8.2.2.4 Impossible Values
Every numeric variable has a possible range. A delivery weight cannot be negative and a moisture percentage cannot be 250. summary() is a quick way to inspect the minimum and maximum:


# Inspect the ranges of the numeric measurements
deliveries |>
  select(weight_tonnes, moisture_pct) |>
  summary()

# Display values outside their possible ranges
deliveries |>
  filter(weight_tonnes <= 0 | moisture_pct > 100) |>
  select(ticket_id, weight_tonnes, moisture_pct)

> # Inspect the ranges of the numeric measurements
> deliveries |>
+   select(weight_tonnes, moisture_pct) |>
+   summary()
 weight_tonnes     moisture_pct    
 Min.   :-12.40   Min.   :  0.086  
 1st Qu.: 32.90   1st Qu.:  8.150  
 Median : 38.80   Median :  9.500  
 Mean   : 36.58   Mean   : 13.220  
 3rd Qu.: 42.90   3rd Qu.: 10.500  
 Max.   : 49.80   Max.   :250.000  
                  NAs    :2        
> 
> # Display values outside their possible ranges
> deliveries |>
+   filter(weight_tonnes <= 0 | moisture_pct > 100) |>
+   select(ticket_id, weight_tonnes, moisture_pct)
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  ticket_id weight_tonnes moisture_pct
  <chr>             <dbl>        <dbl>
1 T0006             -12.4          9.7
2 T0018              41.6        250  
3 T0043               0           10.2



A negative weight may be a sign error or a reversed transaction. A moisture value of 250 may have lost its decimal point. Those are possible explanations, not facts. Correct a value only when the source supports the correction.
Here the synthetic file provides no defensible replacement values. Record that decision by treating the three impossible measurements as missing rather than silently carrying them into later summaries:


# Mark values outside the possible range as missing.
# This records a decision; it does not invent a correction.
deliveries <- deliveries |>
  mutate(
    weight_tonnes = if_else(
      weight_tonnes <= 0,
      NA,
      weight_tonnes
    ),
    moisture_pct = if_else(
      moisture_pct > 100,
      NA,
      moisture_pct
    )
  )

> # Mark values outside the possible range as missing.
> # This records a decision; it does not invent a correction.
> deliveries <- deliveries |>
+   mutate(
+     weight_tonnes = if_else(
+       weight_tonnes <= 0,
+       NA,
+       weight_tonnes
+     ),
+     moisture_pct = if_else(
+       moisture_pct > 100,
+       NA,
+       moisture_pct
+     )
+   )



An extreme value can still be valid. A canola yield of 95 bu/ac is unusual, but it may belong to a very good field. Check it against the source and, if uncertainty remains, compare the analysis with and without it.


8.2.2.5 Inconsistent Categories
Several spellings of the same category produce separate groups. Count each categorical column before using it in group_by():


# Count the crop names as they arrived
deliveries |>
  count(crop, sort = TRUE)

> # Count the crop names as they arrived
> deliveries |>
+   count(crop, sort = TRUE)
# A tibble: 11 × 2
   crop               n
   <chr>          <int>
 1 "Peas"            12
 2 "barley"           9
 3 "Spring wheat"     8
 4 "peas"             7
 5 "Barley"           6
 6 "spring wheat"     5
 7 "canola"           4
 8 "Canola"           3
 9 "Canola "          3
10 "CANOLA"           2
11 "Spring Wheat"     2



Capitalization and spaces can be standardized with string functions:


# Remove extra spaces and use consistent capitalization
deliveries <- deliveries |>
  mutate(crop = str_squish(crop),
         crop = str_to_title(crop))

deliveries |>
  count(crop, sort = TRUE)

> # Remove extra spaces and use consistent capitalization
> deliveries <- deliveries |>
+   mutate(crop = str_squish(crop),
+          crop = str_to_title(crop))
> 
> deliveries |>
+   count(crop, sort = TRUE)
# A tibble: 4 × 2
  crop             n
  <chr>        <int>
1 Peas            19
2 Barley          15
3 Spring Wheat    15
4 Canola          12



Synonyms require an explicit decision. This file contains none after spacing and capitalization are standardized. When documentation says that two labels mean the same thing, put that mapping in the script; for example:


# Reconcile known synonyms while leaving other values unchanged
deliveries <- deliveries |>
  mutate(crop = case_when(
    crop == "Canola/Rapeseed" ~ "Canola",
    crop == "Soybean" ~ "Soybeans",
    TRUE ~ crop
  ))

deliveries |>
  count(crop, sort = TRUE)

> # Reconcile known synonyms while leaving other values unchanged
> deliveries <- deliveries |>
+   mutate(crop = case_when(
+     crop == "Canola/Rapeseed" ~ "Canola",
+     crop == "Soybean" ~ "Soybeans",
+     TRUE ~ crop
+   ))
> 
> deliveries |>
+   count(crop, sort = TRUE)
# A tibble: 4 × 2
  crop             n
  <chr>        <int>
1 Peas            19
2 Barley          15
3 Spring Wheat    15
4 Canola          12



The output is unchanged because those two labels are illustrative and do not occur in this file. A mapping should change data only when the documented source labels are present.


8.2.2.6 Mixed Units
Most moisture readings in the file are percentages near 8 to 15. Three values are below 1, which is not a plausible moisture percentage here; the intended construction of this teaching file confirms that they are proportions such as 0.099 rather than 9.9. The values are numeric, so they produce no parsing error.


# Find moisture readings recorded as decimal proportions
sum(deliveries$moisture_pct < 1, na.rm = TRUE)

deliveries |>
  filter(moisture_pct < 1) |>
  select(ticket_id, moisture_pct)

# Convert decimal proportions to percentages
deliveries <- deliveries |>
  mutate(
    moisture_pct = if_else(
      moisture_pct < 1,
      moisture_pct * 100,
      moisture_pct
    )
  )

> # Find moisture readings recorded as decimal proportions
> sum(deliveries$moisture_pct < 1, na.rm = TRUE)
[1] 3
> 
> deliveries |>
+   filter(moisture_pct < 1) |>
+   select(ticket_id, moisture_pct)
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  ticket_id moisture_pct
  <chr>            <dbl>
1 T0010            0.099
2 T0027            0.086
3 T0050            0.09 
> 
> # Convert decimal proportions to percentages
> deliveries <- deliveries |>
+   mutate(
+     moisture_pct = if_else(
+       moisture_pct < 1,
+       moisture_pct * 100,
+       moisture_pct
+     )
+   )



This rule depends on subject knowledge: a grain moisture value below 1 percent is not plausible here. If the file contains a unit column, use that column in case_when() instead of inferring the unit from the size of the value.


8.2.2.7 Missing Values
R represents a missing value as NA. Most calculations involving NA return NA. The canola trial data has three fields with no rainfall reading:


# Read a file containing three missing rainfall values
trial_data <- read_csv(
  "practice/data/canola_trial.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

mean(trial_data$rainfall_mm)
mean(trial_data$rainfall_mm, na.rm = TRUE)

> # Read a file containing three missing rainfall values
> trial_data <- read_csv(
+   "practice/data/canola_trial.csv",
+   show_col_types = FALSE
+ )
> 
> mean(trial_data$rainfall_mm)
[1] NA
> mean(trial_data$rainfall_mm, na.rm = TRUE)
[1] 229.1017



The first call returns NA because three rainfall values are unknown. The second calculates the mean from the observed values. The argument na.rm = TRUE makes that decision visible. Many Excel functions skip blank cells automatically, so the missing values need to be counted separately there.

Missing values in disguise
A blank cell, "NA", "N/A", "-", "." and -999 may all mean that no value was recorded. The na argument in the first read_csv() call told R which text codes to treat as missing.
Count missing values in every column before deciding what to do with them:


# Count missing values in each column
deliveries |>
  summarise(
    across(everything(), \(x) sum(is.na(x)))
  )

> # Count missing values in each column
> deliveries |>
+   summarise(
+     across(everything(), \(x) sum(is.na(x)))
+   )
# A tibble: 1 × 6
  ticket_id delivery_date  crop weight_tonnes moisture_pct grade
      <int>         <int> <int>         <int>        <int> <int>
1         0             0     0             2            3     1



A numeric code such as -999 is more dangerous. R reads it as a number and includes it in calculations. summary() exposes it as an implausible minimum unless it is converted to NA when the file is read.


Working with missing values
is.na() identifies missing values and drop_na() removes rows that contain them:


# Count missing weights
sum(is.na(deliveries$weight_tonnes))

# Count rows retained after dropping any missing value
deliveries |>
  drop_na() |>
  nrow()

# Count rows retained when only analysis variables matter
deliveries |>
  drop_na(weight_tonnes, moisture_pct) |>
  nrow()

# Calculate a mean from the observed moisture readings
mean(deliveries$moisture_pct, na.rm = TRUE)

> # Count missing weights
> sum(is.na(deliveries$weight_tonnes))
[1] 2
> 
> # Count rows retained after dropping any missing value
> deliveries |>
+   drop_na() |>
+   nrow()
[1] 55
> 
> # Count rows retained when only analysis variables matter
> deliveries |>
+   drop_na(weight_tonnes, moisture_pct) |>
+   nrow()
[1] 56
> 
> # Calculate a mean from the observed moisture readings
> mean(deliveries$moisture_pct, na.rm = TRUE)
[1] 9.606897



The impossible-value decision above created missing values: there are now two missing weights and three missing moisture readings. The mean excludes the flagged moisture value of 250 rather than allowing it to distort the result. Dropping every incomplete row can remove far more data than dropping rows missing the variables used in a particular calculation.


When is dropping safe?
The answer depends on whether the chance a value is missing depends on the value itself. If a rain gauge failed at arbitrary times, the observed days may still represent the season, although there are fewer of them. If low-yielding farms were less likely to report, the remaining records will overstate average yield. In the deliveries file, omitting the three missing moisture readings would be less concerning if records were left blank for administrative reasons than if unusually wet loads were more likely to go unrecorded. Record how many values were missing, which observations were excluded and why the exclusion seemed reasonable.



8.2.2.8 Dates Stored as Text
glimpse() reported delivery_date as <chr> because most rows use 2025-09-07 while two use day/month/year. Text dates sort alphabetically and cannot be used in date arithmetic.
Parse the expected format and inspect the rows that fail. lubridate::ymd() warns when a value does not follow year-month-day order:


# Parse dates written as year-month-day
deliveries_with_dates <- deliveries |>
  mutate(date_parsed = lubridate::ymd(delivery_date))

# Display dates written in a different format
deliveries_with_dates |>
  filter(is.na(date_parsed)) |>
  select(ticket_id, delivery_date)

> # Parse dates written as year-month-day
> deliveries_with_dates <- deliveries |>
+   mutate(date_parsed = lubridate::ymd(delivery_date))
Warning: There was 1 warning in `mutate()`.
ℹ In argument: `date_parsed = lubridate::ymd(delivery_date)`.
Caused by warning:
!  2 failed to parse.
> 
> # Display dates written in a different format
> deliveries_with_dates |>
+   filter(is.na(date_parsed)) |>
+   select(ticket_id, delivery_date)
# A tibble: 2 × 2
  ticket_id delivery_date
  <chr>     <chr>        
1 T0004     15/10/2025   
2 T0047     03/11/2025   



The value 03/11/2025 is ambiguous on its own. The other exceptional value, 15/10/2025, can only be day/month/year, and all deliveries occur from September through November, so the teaching file’s intended convention is day/month/year for both exceptional rows. Parse each stated format and combine the results:


deliveries <- deliveries |>
  mutate(
    delivery_date = coalesce(
      lubridate::ymd(delivery_date, quiet = TRUE),
      lubridate::dmy(delivery_date, quiet = TRUE)
    )
  )

deliveries |>
  select(ticket_id, delivery_date) |>
  filter(ticket_id %in% c("T0004", "T0047"))

glimpse(deliveries$delivery_date)

> deliveries <- deliveries |>
+   mutate(
+     delivery_date = coalesce(
+       lubridate::ymd(delivery_date, quiet = TRUE),
+       lubridate::dmy(delivery_date, quiet = TRUE)
+     )
+   )
> 
> deliveries |>
+   select(ticket_id, delivery_date) |>
+   filter(ticket_id %in% c("T0004", "T0047"))
# A tibble: 2 × 2
  ticket_id delivery_date
  <chr>     <date>       
1 T0004     2025-10-15   
2 T0047     2025-11-03   
> 
> glimpse(deliveries$delivery_date)
 Date[1:61], format: "2025-09-07" "2025-11-25" "2025-09-23" "2025-10-15" "2025-10-16" ...



The choice of day/month/year comes from the file’s construction and context, not from the ambiguous value alone. The final check is that the column is <date>, not <chr> (Section 7.5.1).
Once the checks are complete, write a derived file rather than editing the raw input:
write_csv(
  deliveries,
  "data/processed/grain_deliveries_clean.csv"
)
The raw file remains unchanged, the script records every decision, and rerunning it regenerates the clean file—the same principle as Refresh in Power Query.



A Checklist
Use these checks on a new file:

Use glimpse() to check the dimensions, column names and types.
Write down what one row represents and whether the table is tidy.
Use summary() to inspect the ranges of numeric variables.
Use count() on categorical variables and look for spelling and spacing differences.
Check for exact duplicates and repeated identifiers.
Count NAs in every column and look for other missing-value codes.
Check that units are consistent and dates were read as dates.
Record every correction, exclusion and assumption in the script or Power Query steps.

title: 9  Merging Data
text:
Learning Objectives
The data you need to answer one question often arrive in several tables. For example, suppose we wanted to understand the relationship between RM yields and precipitation. The yield data would come in one table, and the precipitation data would likely come in another. To answer our question, we would need to merge or join these tables.
Throughout this section, we will work with three datasets:
We will do two merges:

title: 9  Merging Data
text:
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

Identify the key that connects two tables.
Distinguish one-to-one, many-to-one and many-to-many relationships.
Merge tables in Excel with Power Query, including a merge that uses two key columns.
Merge tables in R with left_join() and related functions.
Check for unmatched rows and unexpected changes in the row count.



Keys
A key is a column, or set of columns, used to identify and match rows across datasets. When we merge, we say that we merge on the key. The key must be present in both datasets.
In the three tables above, the keys for the two merges are:

RM yields to RM lookup: RM.
The resulting dataset to weather-station data: weather station and year.



One-to-one, many-to-one and many-to-many
There are three types of merges:






Figure 9.1: Three kinds of merge. Each line connects a grades row to the row it matches.




One-to-one (1:1). Each key value appears once in both tables. Grades and attendance both have one row per student-class, so the merged table has the same number of rows as either input.
Many-to-one (n:1). Values in the key column may repeat in one dataset but are unique in the other. In this example, students take many classes, so each student appears multiple times in the table on the left. Each class has a single professor, however, so each class appears only once in the table on the right.
Many-to-many (n:n). Values in the key column repeat in both datasets. In the figure, students take multiple classes (the table on the left), and each class can have multiple teaching assistants (the table on the right).

Before joining, decide which relationship you expect. Then compare the row counts before and after.
Both of our merges will be many-to-one:

The RM yields dataset contains many observations for the same RM, but the RM lookup contains only one row for each RM.
The merged dataset from step 1 contains many observations with the same closest weather station and year, but the weather-station dataset contains only one observation for each station and year.

title: 9  Merging Data
text:
9.1 Merging in Excel
In Chapter 2, we used XLOOKUP to bring values from one table into another (Section 2.2). That approach is useful for a quick lookup. Here, we will use Power Query because it records the merge as a repeatable series of steps and can match on several columns directly.
Begin by importing rm_yields_2015_2024.csv and rm_lookup.csv with Data > Get Data > From Text/CSV > Transform Data. In the Power Query editor:

Load the RM yield data using Power Query, transforming the data to longer format as we did before.
Choose Power Query, select import csv, and select the RM lookup table.
Select transform data. You will now see two queries on your left hand side (Figure 9.2).
Select the first query (rm_yields_2015_2024) and then click Home > Merge Queries.







Figure 9.2: The two queries loaded, with the yield data in long format and Merge queries on the ribbon.




In the pop up menu (Figure 9.3) select rm_lookup as the right table to merge.
Select the key to merge on in each table by clicking its column heading: RM in the yields table and RM_Number in the lookup table.
Keep Left Outer as the join kind. This keeps every yield observation and adds information wherever the lookup contains a matching RM.
Check the number of matching rows reported at the bottom of the dialog – here every one of the 15,478 yield observations finds a match – then choose OK.







Figure 9.3: The Merge dialog: the two tables, the key selected in each, the join kind, and the match count along the bottom.




The merged data arrives packed into a single new column whose every entry reads [Table] (Figure 9.4). Expand it using the double-arrow icon in its header: tick the columns you want (the RM name, census division, population and closest weather station) and untick Use original column name as prefix so the columns keep their own names.







Figure 9.4: After the merge, the lookup columns sit folded inside a [Table] column. The double-arrow icon in its header expands them. Do not click a [Table] link itself – that drills into that one row’s table and discards the rest.









Figure 9.5: After expanding: the lookup columns sit beside every yield observation, and the row count has not changed.



Now you should see the RM lookup data merged with the RM yield data. We can now repeat the same process to merge once again with the station data: import station_precip.csv the same way, so a third query appears (Figure 9.6). The only difference is that we are now going to merge on both the station name and the year (Figure 9.7). Select Weather_Station and then Ctrl-click Year in the top table, and Station then Ctrl-click Year in the bottom one – the small 1 and 2 beside the headings show the matching order.






Figure 9.6: The station precipitation data imported as a third query.









Figure 9.7: The second Merge dialog, with the station column selected in each table; Ctrl-clicking Year in each adds it as the second key. Station and year together identify the right precipitation value.



After expanding the precipitation column and choosing Close & load, every yield observation carries its RM’s name, closest station, and that station’s growing-season precipitation for the right year.


Checking the merge
After each merge, compare the number of rows with the original yields table. A many-to-one left merge should retain the same number of rows. Filter the expanded columns for null to find observations that did not match, and check several rows against the source tables.
Power Query also offers Inner, Full Outer and Left Anti joins. These correspond to the R joins introduced below. A Left Anti join is particularly useful for listing rows that have no match before completing the merge.

title: 9  Merging Data
text:
9.2 Merging in R
In tidyverse we merge data with join functions. There are four different types of joins depending on which data we want to keep in the merged file. Suppose we have two datasets y and x:

left_join(x, y, by) keeps every row of x whether it has a match in y or not. But does not keep rows in y that don’t have a match.
inner_join(x, y, by) keeps only rows that matched in both tables.
full_join(x, y, by) keeps every row from both tables, regardless of whether there is a match.
anti_join(x, y, by) returns the rows of x that have no match in y. It is useful for finding failed matches before a join.

The by argument specifies the keys we merge on. It can be a single column name or a vector of names.
Read the three files and inspect their columns:


## Load pacakges
library(tidyverse)

# Read the three tables
yields <- read_csv(
  "practice/data/rm_yields_2015_2024.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

rms <- read_csv(
  "practice/data/rm_lookup.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

rain <- read_csv(
  "practice/data/station_precip.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

> ## Load pacakges
> library(tidyverse)
── Attaching core tidyverse packages ──────────────────────── tidyverse 2.0.0 ──
✔ dplyr     1.2.1     ✔ readr     2.2.0
✔ forcats   1.0.1     ✔ stringr   1.6.0
✔ ggplot2   4.0.3     ✔ tibble    3.3.1
✔ lubridate 1.9.5     ✔ tidyr     1.3.2
✔ purrr     1.2.2     
── Conflicts ────────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ──
✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter()
✖ dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
ℹ Use the conflicted package (<http://conflicted.r-lib.org/>) to force all conflicts to become errors
> 
> # Read the three tables
> yields <- read_csv(
+   "practice/data/rm_yields_2015_2024.csv",
+   show_col_types = FALSE
+ )
> 
> rms <- read_csv(
+   "practice/data/rm_lookup.csv",
+   show_col_types = FALSE
+ )
> 
> rain <- read_csv(
+   "practice/data/station_precip.csv",
+   show_col_types = FALSE
+ )



We can now use left_join() takes two data frames and a by argument that identifies the key. If a key has different names in the two tables, write join_by(left_name == right_name); a column with the same name on both sides is written once. The older by = c("left_name" = "right_name") form still appears in other people’s code.
Before joining, check that the columns expected to identify one row are actually unique:


rms |>
  count(rm_number) |>
  filter(n > 1)

rain |>
  count(station, year) |>
  filter(n > 1)

> rms |>
+   count(rm_number) |>
+   filter(n > 1)
Error: Must group by variables found in `.data`.
✖ Column `rm_number` is not found.
> 
> rain |>
+   count(station, year) |>
+   filter(n > 1)
Error: Must group by variables found in `.data`.
Column `station` is not found.
Column `year` is not found.



Both checks return empty tibbles. A key is only a key if each combination occurs no more than once on the side where uniqueness is expected.

First join: yields and the RM lookup
The RM column is called rm in the yields table and rm_number in the lookup. Check for unmatched RMs, perform the join and compare the row counts:


# List RM numbers that have no lookup row
yields |>
  anti_join(rms, by = join_by(rm == rm_number)) |>
  distinct(rm)

# Add the RM information and nearest station
with_station <- yields |>
  left_join(rms,
            by = join_by(rm == rm_number),
            relationship = "many-to-one")

nrow(yields)
nrow(with_station)

> # List RM numbers that have no lookup row
> yields |>
+   anti_join(rms, by = join_by(rm == rm_number)) |>
+   distinct(rm)
Error: Join columns in `x` must be present in the data.
✖ Problem with `rm`.
> 
> # Add the RM information and nearest station
> with_station <- yields |>
+   left_join(rms,
+             by = join_by(rm == rm_number),
+             relationship = "many-to-one")
Error: Join columns in `x` must be present in the data.
✖ Problem with `rm`.
> 
> nrow(yields)
[1] 2950
> nrow(with_station)
Error: object 'with_station' not found



The anti_join() returns an empty tibble, so every RM has a match. yields has 2,950 rows and so does with_station, which is what a many-to-one join should give. The relationship = "many-to-one" argument records what we expect and makes left_join() stop if the lookup contains more than one row for an RM.
In R, text keys are sensitive to both case and spaces. For example, "canola", "Canola" and "Canola " are three different keys. These differences have to be reconciled before the join (Section 8.2.2.5).


A failed match on purpose
The complete rain table matches every station-year. To see how the joins differ when data are missing, temporarily remove 2021:


rain_short <- rain |>
  filter(year != 2021)

# Which yield rows no longer have rain?
with_station |>
  anti_join(
    rain_short,
    by = join_by(weather_station == station, year)
  ) |>
  count(weather_station)

# A left join keeps all 2,950 yield rows,
# including 295 rows with missing rain.
with_station |>
  left_join(
    rain_short,
    by = join_by(weather_station == station, year)
  ) |>
  filter(is.na(precip_may_aug_mm)) |>
  nrow()

# An inner join drops those 295 rows.
with_station |>
  inner_join(
    rain_short,
    by = join_by(weather_station == station, year)
  ) |>
  nrow()

# A full join also keeps a right-side row
# that has no yield-side match.
rain_extra <- rain_short |>
  add_row(
    station = "Course example",
    year = 2025,
    precip_may_aug_mm = 200,
    days_missing = 0
  )

with_station |>
  full_join(
    rain_extra,
    by = join_by(weather_station == station, year)
  ) |>
  filter(weather_station == "Course example") |>
  select(year, weather_station, rm, canola)

> rain_short <- rain |>
+   filter(year != 2021)
Error: ℹ In argument: `year != 2021`.
Caused by error in `year != 2021`:
! comparison (!=) is possible only for atomic and list types
> 
> # Which yield rows no longer have rain?
> with_station |>
+   anti_join(
+     rain_short,
+     by = join_by(weather_station == station, year)
+   ) |>
+   count(weather_station)
Error: object 'with_station' not found
> 
> # A left join keeps all 2,950 yield rows,
> # including 295 rows with missing rain.
> with_station |>
+   left_join(
+     rain_short,
+     by = join_by(weather_station == station, year)
+   ) |>
+   filter(is.na(precip_may_aug_mm)) |>
+   nrow()
Error: object 'with_station' not found
> 
> # An inner join drops those 295 rows.
> with_station |>
+   inner_join(
+     rain_short,
+     by = join_by(weather_station == station, year)
+   ) |>
+   nrow()
Error: object 'with_station' not found
> 
> # A full join also keeps a right-side row
> # that has no yield-side match.
> rain_extra <- rain_short |>
+   add_row(
+     station = "Course example",
+     year = 2025,
+     precip_may_aug_mm = 200,
+     days_missing = 0
+   )
Error: object 'rain_short' not found
> 
> with_station |>
+   full_join(
+     rain_extra,
+     by = join_by(weather_station == station, year)
+   ) |>
+   filter(weather_station == "Course example") |>
+   select(year, weather_station, rm, canola)
Error: object 'with_station' not found



anti_join() identifies the failed keys, left_join() makes the missing matches visible as NA, and inner_join() silently removes them. The final full_join() also retains the deliberately added rain row that has no yield-side match, filling its yield columns with NA.


Second join: add the rain
The second key has two parts. The station column is called weather_station on the left and station on the right; year has the same name in both tables.


# Find station-years with no precipitation row
with_station |>
  anti_join(rain,
            by = join_by(weather_station == station, year)) |>
  distinct(weather_station, year)

# Add precipitation for the matching station and year
merged <- with_station |>
  left_join(rain,
            by = join_by(weather_station == station, year),
            relationship = "many-to-one")

nrow(merged)

> # Find station-years with no precipitation row
> with_station |>
+   anti_join(rain,
+             by = join_by(weather_station == station, year)) |>
+   distinct(weather_station, year)
Error: object 'with_station' not found
> 
> # Add precipitation for the matching station and year
> merged <- with_station |>
+   left_join(rain,
+             by = join_by(weather_station == station, year),
+             relationship = "many-to-one")
Error: object 'with_station' not found
> 
> nrow(merged)
Error: object 'merged' not found



Again there are no unmatched keys and the row count remains 2,950.


The row-count trap
Now leave year out of the key:


Error in eval(e, envir) : object 'with_station' not found


# This key is incomplete: every row matches ten years of rain
with_station |>
  left_join(rain,
            by = join_by(weather_station == station)) |>
  nrow()

# State the expected relationship to turn
# the warning into an error.
try(
  with_station |>
    left_join(
      rain,
      by = join_by(weather_station == station),
      relationship = "many-to-one"
    )
)

> # This key is incomplete: every row matches ten years of rain
> with_station |>
+   left_join(rain,
+             by = join_by(weather_station == station)) |>
+   nrow()
Error: object 'with_station' not found
> 
> # State the expected relationship to turn
> # the warning into an error.
> try(
+   with_station |>
+     left_join(
+       rain,
+       by = join_by(weather_station == station),
+       relationship = "many-to-one"
+     )
+ )



Each yield row matches all ten years for its station, so 2,950 rows become 29,500. By default, dplyr warns about the unexpected many-to-many relationship. When relationship = "many-to-one" states what was intended, the same mistake becomes an error and the analysis stops. Excel’s station-only XLOOKUP makes the mistake differently: it returns only the first matching year and gives no warning.

title: 9  Merging Data
text:
9.3 What the Merge Gives You
The merged table has one row per RM-year, with yield and precipitation beside one another:


# Display the columns used in the analysis
merged |>
  select(year, rm, rm_name, canola,
         weather_station, precip_may_aug_mm)

# Calculate annual mean yield and precipitation
merged |>
  filter(!is.na(canola)) |>
  summarise(
    canola_bu_ac = mean(canola),
    rain_mm = mean(precip_may_aug_mm),
    max_days_missing = max(days_missing),
    .by = year
  )

# Count yield values excluded from those means
merged |>
  summarise(missing_canola = sum(is.na(canola)))

# Describe association, not causation
merged |>
  summarise(
    yield_rain_correlation = cor(
      canola,
      precip_may_aug_mm,
      use = "complete.obs"
    )
  )

> # Display the columns used in the analysis
> merged |>
+   select(year, rm, rm_name, canola,
+          weather_station, precip_may_aug_mm)
Error: object 'merged' not found
> 
> # Calculate annual mean yield and precipitation
> merged |>
+   filter(!is.na(canola)) |>
+   summarise(
+     canola_bu_ac = mean(canola),
+     rain_mm = mean(precip_may_aug_mm),
+     max_days_missing = max(days_missing),
+     .by = year
+   )
Error: object 'merged' not found
> 
> # Count yield values excluded from those means
> merged |>
+   summarise(missing_canola = sum(is.na(canola)))
Error: object 'merged' not found
> 
> # Describe association, not causation
> merged |>
+   summarise(
+     yield_rain_correlation = cor(
+       canola,
+       precip_may_aug_mm,
+       use = "complete.obs"
+     )
+   )
Error: object 'merged' not found



Across RM-years, wetter observations tend to have higher canola yield, but the relationship is loose: the correlation is about 0.41. The annual table also resists a simple rainfall story. Both 2021 and 2024 have low average yields despite ordinary or above-average rainfall. These data cannot say why. Testing whether heat contributed would require temperature data; explaining the remaining differences would require other variables as well.
The annual means exclude 46 RM-years with no published canola yield. They also average rainfall over RM rows, so a station serving more RMs receives more weight than a station serving fewer RMs. The merge has further limits that should be recorded in the project’s README. The median RM is 62 km from its assigned station, one quarter are more than 85 km away, and the maximum is 161 km, so station rainfall is a coarse proxy for rainfall across an RM. Some station-years also have many missing daily observations—up to 25 days in this file—and their seasonal totals sum only the available days, which biases those totals downward.

title: 10  Graphing Best Practices
text:
Learning Objectives
A good chart tells a story. It draws the reader’s attention to a pattern, comparison, or relationship in the data and leaves them with something worth remembering. Charts do this by turning numbers into visual comparisons of position, length, area, or colour. When those comparisons make the story in the data easier to see, a chart is more useful than a table of numbers.
One of the best charts I’ve seen1 tells the story of Napoleon’s invasion and subsequent retreat from Russia in 1812 (Figure 10.1).
The width of the band represents the size of the army, its position follows the route of advance and retreat, and the line below records temperature and dates during the retreat. The tan band begins with 422,000 men crossing into Russia. The black band returns with 10,000. Think of all the information that is embodied in this graph – the size of the army, where they travelled, their dates of travel (on their retreat), and temperature. A reader could never take in this type of information in a set of data tables.
Figure 10.2 was published by the Georgia Department of Public Health in May 2020. It appears to show COVID-19 cases falling steadily in the five counties with the most confirmed cases.
The dates along the horizontal axis are out of order. They were sorted by case count, so the decline is built into the chart rather than present in the data. The labels contain the information needed to catch the problem, but only a reader who checks every date will find it.
These examples set the two jobs of a chart. It should make the comparison easy to see, and it should represent the data honestly.

title: 10  Graphing Best Practices
text:
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

State the comparison a chart is meant to show.
Choose a chart type that fits that comparison.
Label a chart so that it can be read without its maker present.
Remove clutter and use colour, text and legends deliberately.
Identify axis choices and chart forms that can mislead a reader.

title: 10  Graphing Best Practices
text:
10.1 General Principles

Decide whether a chart actually helps
First, you need to decide whether you actually need a graph to get the point across to your audience. Sometimes tables, or just text, do a better job. For example, if I wanted to compare US and Canadian wheat production, I could do so through Figure 10.3. Or I could simply write: In 2024 the United States produced 53.7 million tonnes of wheat and Canada produced 34.9 million. Turning this text into a graph only distracts the reader.








Figure 10.3: Two values that are easier to state in a sentence. Source: approximate 2024/25 marketing-year figures from U.S. Department of Agriculture (2025).





However, if we wanted to give the reader a sense of Canada’s place among the world’s leading producers of wheat, then Figure 10.4 would do that better than a table or text.








Figure 10.4: The top fifteen wheat-producing countries, 2024/25. Canada is highlighted. Source: approximate 2024/25 marketing-year figures from U.S. Department of Agriculture (2025).







Check the scale and order
Charts can mislead while still plotting correct numbers. Figure 10.2 misled audiences by changing the order of the dates. There are many other ways to mislead. A lot of this comes down to altering the way data is presented relative to the audience’s expectations. In Figure 10.2 we expect dates to be ordered chronologically.
One easy way to mislead is to start your vertical axis at a number other than zero. We generally expect that the relative size of bars on a bar chart reflects the relative differences in the values being plotted. But when the vertical axis starts at a number other than zero this isn’t true.
Consider the two panels in Figure 10.5. Both show the same five malting barley varieties, with yields from 103 to 114 bushels per acre. In panel A, the vertical axis starts at 100. This makes the bar for CDC Copeland appear to be about one-fifth the size of the bar for CDC Churchill. In panel B, we see that the bar for Copeland is 90% the size of the bar for Churchill, reflecting that Copeland’s yields were roughly 90% of Churchill’s in the trials.











(a) A. Axis starting at 100











(b) B. Axis starting at zero







Figure 10.5: The same five yields with the axis beginning at 100 and at zero. Source: Saskatchewan Ministry of Agriculture (2025).



Excel chooses axis bounds automatically and may produce panel A by default when the values are close together. For a column chart, right-click the value axis, choose Format Axis, and set the Minimum bound to 0. The zero baseline displays the size difference honestly, but it does not establish that small differences between trial averages are meaningful.
Line charts are different. A line shows position rather than length, so its vertical axis does not always need to begin at zero. The displayed range should still be wide enough that ordinary movement does not look like a crisis.


Use descriptive labels
Every chart should tell the reader what they are looking at. At a minimum, this usually means clear labels for the horizontal and vertical axes, along with tick-mark labels that make the scale easy to interpret. Labels should also make the units clear. If a chart shows yield, for example, the reader should not have to guess whether it is measured in bushels per acre, tonnes per hectare, or something else.
There is some art to labelling a chart. Too little information leaves the reader guessing, while too much text can make the chart feel cluttered. Include the information the reader needs to interpret the figure, but avoid labels that simply repeat information already obvious from the chart.
When a figure will appear in a report, it generally looks best to leave the chart title blank in your statistical software and give the figure a caption in the document itself. For example, if you create a chart in R and insert it into a Word report, you can leave the title blank in R and use Word’s captioning function instead. This keeps figure titles consistent with the formatting and numbering used throughout the report.


Remove clutter
Gridlines, borders, markers and decoration all compete with the data. Keep the elements that help the comparison and remove the rest. Some formatting that I would suggest (some of this is personal preference):

A minimal number of horizontal gridlines, spaced at intervals of 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 25, 50 or 100 (not 3, 7 or 12).
No vertical gridlines, except for scatter plots.
When dealing with large numbers, put the vertical axis in thousands or millions.












(a) A. Cluttered











(b) B. Reduced







Figure 10.6: The same four series before and after unnecessary chart elements are removed. Source: Saskatchewan Crop Insurance Corporation (2025).



Three-dimensional effects distort length and area. Patterned fills were useful when charts had to be printed in black and white, but on a screen they make the bars harder to read.











(a) A. Patterned fills











(b) B. Flat fills







Figure 10.7: Patterned and flat fills applied to the same bars. Source: Saskatchewan Crop Insurance Corporation (2025).





Label lines directly
A legend makes the reader match each line to a separate key. When there is room, put the series name at the end of the line instead. Admittedly, both of the panels in Figure 10.8 are a bit busy. But at least in panel B, you can easily identify which line corresponds to a particular variety.








A. The lines identified with a legend.







B. Labels placed beside the lines.






Figure 10.8: Western Canadian barley variety shares of acreage, 2008–2025. Source: Canadian Grain Commission (2025).



Legends are still useful when direct labels would overlap, or when the same symbols appear in several panels.


Annotate what needs explanation
A short note within the chart can explain an unusual point or change, or draw the reader’s attention to an important part of the story in the data (as in panel B of Figure 10.9). Use notes sparingly, however: too many can clutter the chart and obscure the very patterns they are meant to highlight (as in panel A of Figure 10.9).











(a) A. Every movement annotated











(b) B. The unusual movement annotated







Figure 10.9: Urea prices with many annotations and with one; indicative annual US Gulf prices, USD per tonne. Source: author’s indicative figures; for the underlying urea price series see World Bank (2025).





Adding more information to charts
While most charts are two dimensional, there are ways of bringing in more information, through colours, shapes and sizes. Figure 10.1 is a great example of artfully condensing a considerable amount of information into a single plot. Another example is Figure 10.10, where the point size represents spring wheat seeded acres in addition to wheat and barley yield, and the point colour marks each risk zone’s soil zone.








Figure 10.10: Wheat yield, barley yield, spring wheat seeded acres and soil zone for Saskatchewan risk zones, 2025. Source: Saskatchewan Crop Insurance Corporation (2025).





Medical journals have taken this idea further with the visual abstract, a one-page graphic that summarizes a whole study. Figure 10.11 is the BMJ’s visual abstract for a study of chronic traumatic encephalopathy in former NFL players (Daneshvar et al. 2026). Notice how much of this chapter it uses. The answer comes first, in a sentence. Exact values sit in a small table. The dot circles scale their area to the number of donors at each CTE stage, so the concentration of dementia cases at stages III and IV is visible before you read a single number. The photo carries no data; it is there to say what the graphic is about at a glance.






Figure 10.11: The BMJ’s visual abstract for a study of CTE in former NFL players. Source: Daneshvar et al. (2026), visual abstract, © 2026 BMJ Publishing Group Ltd.



However, one should be wary of trying to cram too much information into a single plot. A particular no-no is to use two different vertical axes on the same plot, as in Figure 10.12. This is a poor choice for a number of reasons, notably that the audience has to work to understand which line corresponds to which axis. It is almost always better to plot these as two separate charts.











(a) A. First right-hand scale











(b) B. Second right-hand scale







Figure 10.12: The same two series under two choices for the right-hand axis. Source: Saskatchewan Crop Insurance Corporation (2025).





Use colour for a reason
Colour can distinguish groups, show an ordered scale or draw attention to one observation. For example, in Figure 10.4 we highlighted Canada in the plot, as I was assuming our audience would be Canadian. If we were presenting on the possible impacts on world wheat markets of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, then we might want to highlight Russia and Ukraine. In Figure 10.10, we denoted different soil zones with different colours.
Choose colours that remain distinguishable for readers with colour-vision deficiencies and when printed in grey. It is also best practice to distinguish series by colour and some other means, where possible. For example, if you have three lines on a graph, you can use colours, direct labels, and dashes to differentiate them. Again, much depends on your particular data. In Figure 10.14 the lines on the graph are all very distinct, so direct labels are enough to allow the audience to distinguish each line across the whole graph. If the lines intersected each other more, we might want to add different dashing to the lines.

title: 10  Graphing Best Practices
text:
10.2 Types of Charts

Bar charts: compare categories
A bar chart compares a value across categories such as yield by crop, acres by region or revenue by customer. Sort bars by value unless the categories have a natural order (as in the example of Figure 10.2, where bars should have been ordered chronologically). Start the value axis at zero. Note that bar charts often look better when horizontal, particularly where there are a large number of categories.











(a) A. Vertical











(b) B. Horizontal







Figure 10.13: The same five varieties drawn with vertical and horizontal bars. Source: Saskatchewan Ministry of Agriculture (2025).





Line charts: show change over time
A line chart shows movement over a continuous scale, usually time. The connection between points implies that the order and interval have meaning. Most commonly they are used with a measure of time on the horizontal axis. Do not connect unordered categories such as Barley, Canola and Oats with a line.








Figure 10.14: Average crop yield by year, with labels at the right-hand ends of the lines; provincial averages weighted by acres. Source: Saskatchewan Crop Insurance Corporation (2025).







Scatter plots: compare two numeric variables
A scatter plot places one numeric variable on each axis and one observation at each point.








Figure 10.15: Spring wheat and barley yield in Saskatchewan’s 21 risk zones. Source: Saskatchewan Crop Insurance Corporation (2025).





The points rise from left to right in this 2025 cross-section. Both crops in a zone shared the same growing season, so the pattern says little by itself about whether zones that are good for wheat are generally good for barley. Module 7 develops the numerical tools for describing relationships like this.


Stacked and grouped bars: compare composition
A stacked bar shows a total and its components.








Figure 10.16: Seeded acres by crop and year, drawn as stacked bars. Source: Saskatchewan Crop Insurance Corporation (2025).





One issue with stacked bar charts is that only the bottom segment and the total of each bar can be easily compared. In Figure 10.16 it is difficult to compare the seeded acreage of canola over time.
Grouped bars give each component a zero baseline, but they become crowded as the number of groups grows, making it hard to compare different crops within one year and crops across time.








Figure 10.17: The same acreage data drawn as grouped bars. Source: Saskatchewan Crop Insurance Corporation (2025).





An alternative is plotting the crops in separate plots, as in Figure 10.18.








Figure 10.18: The acreage data divided into one panel per crop. Source: Saskatchewan Crop Insurance Corporation (2025).







Pie charts: show a simple share
A pie chart shows parts of a total. Most authorities on charts really dislike pie charts. One reason is that angles and areas are harder to compare than lengths, so a bar chart is usually a better way of visualizing differences. Labels on pie charts are also somewhat hard to get right, particularly when pie slices are small. If a pie chart is used, keep the number of slices small and label them directly with percentages.











(a) A. Pie











(b) B. Bars







Figure 10.19: The same four acreage shares shown as a pie and as bars. Source: Saskatchewan Crop Insurance Corporation (2025).





Ranges, trend lines and reference lines
Charts often are used to show averages. However, one might also want to give the audience some sense of the variation in the data. This can be done through shading around the line. The shaded area might represent the minimum and maximum, or particular percentiles. The definition of the shaded area should be clearly stated in the figure caption.
In Figure 10.20 we use shading to indicate the 10th and 90th percentiles of the risk-zone yields.








Figure 10.20: Average spring wheat yield, with the band covering the 10th to 90th percentiles of risk-zone yields in each year. Source: Saskatchewan Crop Insurance Corporation (2025).





A fitted line summarizes the trend in a scatter plot, as in Figure 10.21. I tend to advocate against trend lines – if a trend is not so obvious that it can be seen in the raw data, why include the line?








Figure 10.21: The wheat-barley scatter plot with a fitted straight line added. Source: Saskatchewan Crop Insurance Corporation (2025).





A reference line can show an average, a target, a break-even value or last year’s result, as in Figure 10.22. Include one when the comparison against it is the point of the chart: yields against the five-year average, prices against break-even. If the reader is not meant to compare each bar against that value, the line is just another element competing for attention, and the information may belong in the caption or the surrounding text instead.








Figure 10.22: Canola yield by year against its five-year average. Source: Saskatchewan Crop Insurance Corporation (2025).

title: 10  Graphing Best Practices
text:
Other resources
