text:
Questions 71–80 · Saskatchewan RM Crop Yields (long file)
For this section use the long file rm_yields_1990_2025.csv, which has the crop name in its own Crop column so you can group by crop.

Question 91
Using the Saskatchewan RM Crop Yields dataset (long file).
(a) Build a PivotTable of average yield by crop for 2023 (Year in Filters = 2023, Crop on Rows, Yield as Average). Rank the crops.
(b) Look at the ranked averages. If one crop’s value looks out of line with the others, identify it and explain why it is so different.
(c) Explain what a reader would wrongly conclude if they took the ranking at face value.
(d) Add Unit to Filters and set it to bu/ac. Identify the highest and lowest crop now.
(e) Explain why the filtered comparison is the fair one.


Answer



Lentils ≈1314, Oats ≈71, Barley ≈55, Spring Wheat ≈43, Peas ≈34, Canola ≈34, Durum ≈30, Flax ≈20.


Lentils — reported in lb/ac, everything else in bu/ac.


That lentils out-yield oats ~18× — a unit artifact, not a real yield difference.


Filtered to bu/ac: Oats highest (≈71), Flax lowest (≈20).


All crops then share one unit, so the magnitudes are comparable. 📗 Answer workbook — the source data on one tab and a real PivotTable on another. Open it in Excel and the field list is live, so you can drag the fields around and see how the grid changes.





Question 92
Using the Saskatchewan RM Crop Yields dataset (long file).
(a) Build a PivotTable with Year on Rows and Crop on Columns (Yield as Average, Unit filtered to bu/ac).
(b) Compare canola in 2021 versus 2023, and describe the size of the change in plain language.
(c) Scan the 2021 row across all crops. Describe what you notice.
(d) Explain how a whole low row (a year) differs, in cause, from a single low column value (one crop in one year).
(e) State what the grid lets you conclude about 2021, and why.


Answer



Year × Crop grid of average yields.


Canola in 2021 (≈21.9) is about one-third lower than 2023 (≈33.9) — a large drop.


Every crop’s 2021 average is low, not just canola.


A low row = a broad cause hitting all crops that year; a single low column value = a crop-specific problem that year.


2021 was a broad, region-wide low year — the whole row is depressed, so the cause was general rather than crop-specific. 📗 Answer workbook — the source data on one tab and a real PivotTable on another. Open it in Excel and the field list is live, so you can drag the fields around and see how the grid changes.





Question 93
Using the Saskatchewan RM Crop Yields dataset (long file).
(a) Build a single PivotTable with Crop on Rows and Year on Columns (Yield as Average, Unit = bu/ac), then filter the columns to just 2019 and 2025.
(b) For each crop, read the 2019 and 2025 values and compute the change (2025 minus 2019).
(c) State which crop rose the most in absolute bu/ac between those two years.
(d) Explain why the crop that rose most in absolute terms is not necessarily the one that rose most in relative terms.
(e) Describe how you would use the PivotTable output to compute a relative change for each crop.


Answer



One Crop × Year pivot, columns filtered to 2019 and 2025.


2025 minus 2019 per crop (e.g. Oats 97.5 − 89.4 ≈ 8.1; Barley 72.8 − 68.6 ≈ 4.2; Canola 43.9 − 40.8 ≈ 3.1).


Oats rose most in absolute bu/ac (~8).


Oats already yield the most, so a big absolute gain can be a small percentage; a lower-yielding crop’s smaller gain could be a larger percentage.


Divide each crop’s change by its 2019 value to get the relative (percent) change. 📗 Answer workbook — the source data on one tab and a real PivotTable on another. Open it in Excel and the field list is live, so you can drag the fields around and see how the grid changes.





Question 94
Using the Saskatchewan RM Crop Yields dataset (long file).
(a) Build a PivotTable of the count of reporting RMs for canola each year (Crop filtered to Canola, Year on Rows, Yield as Count).
(b) State roughly how many RMs report canola in a typical recent year.
(c) Explain what a change in the yearly count would tell you about reporting coverage, using counts only.
(d) Explain why you would use Count (not Average) for this particular question.
(e) State, in one sentence, the difference between a PivotTable Count and a PivotTable Average of the same field.


Answer



Year on Rows, Yield → Values set to Count.


About 290 RMs report canola in recent years.


A stable count means steady coverage; a dip would signal fewer RMs reporting that year.


Count answers “how many RMs reported,” whereas Average answers “what did they yield” — here you want the number of reports.


Count tallies how many values there are; Average gives their mean — one measures coverage, the other level. 📗 Answer workbook — the source data on one tab and a real PivotTable on another. Open it in Excel and the field list is live, so you can drag the fields around and see how the grid changes.





Question 95
Using the Saskatchewan RM Crop Yields dataset (long file).
(a) Build a PivotTable with Crop on Rows and Yield as both Average and Count (two value columns), filtered to bu/ac, for 2023.
(b) Identify which crop has the most reports and which has the fewest.
(c) Explain why a crop with fewer reports has a less reliable average, using the count column.
(d) Explain how having Count next to Average in the same PivotTable helps you judge each average.
(e) State, in one sentence, why you would show both Average and Count when presenting a by-crop summary.


Answer



Crop on Rows; Yield → Average and Yield → Count.


Report the most- and fewest-reported crops from the count column (e.g. Spring Wheat/Barley high, Flax/Durum lower in 2023).


A crop with fewer reporting RMs has an average built on less data, so it is more easily swayed by a few RMs.


The count tells you how much data supports each average, so you know which averages to trust more.


The average states the level and the count states its support — together they let a reader weigh each figure. 📗 Answer workbook — the source data on one tab and a real PivotTable on another. Open it in Excel and the field list is live, so you can drag the fields around and see how the grid changes.





Question 96
Using the Saskatchewan RM Crop Yields dataset (long file).
(a) Build a PivotTable with Crop on Rows and Year on Columns (Yield as Average, bu/ac), covering 2019–2023.
(b) Read across the Canola row. Identify its lowest year in that span.
(c) Read across the Barley row. Does it share the same lowest year?
(d) Explain what it means when two different crop rows share their lowest year in the same grid.
(e) State, in one sentence, why a Crop × Year grid is an efficient way to spot a year that hit many crops at once.


Answer



Crop × Year grid.


Canola’s lowest in 2019–2023 is 2021 (≈21.9).


Yes — barley’s lowest in that span is also 2021.


Both crops bottoming in the same year points to a shared, broad cause that year.


The grid lets you scan a single column (year) across all crop rows at once, so a broadly bad year stands out immediately. 📗 Answer workbook — the source data on one tab and a real PivotTable on another. Open it in Excel and the field list is live, so you can drag the fields around and see how the grid changes.





Question 97
Using the Saskatchewan RM Crop Yields dataset (long file).
(a) Build a PivotTable of average yield by crop across all years, with Yield added to Values a second time as Count (Crop on Rows, bu/ac).
(b) Rank the crops by their long-run average.
(c) In the 2023-only ranking, Oats is the highest-yielding crop and Flax the lowest (among bu/ac crops). Compare that to your all-years ranking — is the order the same, and why might a single-year ranking differ from the long-run one?
(d) Using the Count column, say which crops have the fewest reports, and explain why a thin count makes a crop’s long-run rank less trustworthy.
(e) State, in one sentence, when you would prefer an all-years average over a single-year average.


Answer



Crop on Rows, Yield Average, all years.


Oats highest, then Barley, Spring Wheat, Durum/Peas/Canola, Flax lowest (bu/ac).


Largely the same order (Oats > Barley > Spring Wheat > … > Flax), with minor shuffles among the middle crops.


Durum (≈7,137 reports) and Flax (≈8,077) are the thinnest; Spring Wheat (≈10,534) and Barley (≈10,401) the fullest. A crop reported by fewer RMs has its average built on less data, so its rank can move on a handful of results.


Use the all-years average when you want a stable, typical ranking rather than one year’s result. 📗 Answer workbook — the source data on one tab and a real PivotTable on another. Open it in Excel and the field list is live, so you can drag the fields around and see how the grid changes.





Question 98
Using the Saskatchewan RM Crop Yields dataset (long file).
(a) Build a PivotTable with Year on Rows and Yield as Average for Oats only (Crop filtered to Oats), 2019–2025.
(b) Identify the highest and lowest years for oats in that span.
(c) Explain how filtering to one crop before pivoting by year isolates that crop’s year-to-year pattern.
(d) Explain why you must set the aggregation to Average (not Sum) for a yield question like this.
(e) State, in one sentence, why summing yields across RMs would produce a meaningless number.


Answer



Year on Rows, Yield Average, Crop = Oats.


Highest ≈ 2025 (~97), lowest ≈ 2021 (~45).


With only oats in the pivot, the year rows show oats’ own averages, uncontaminated by other crops.


Average gives the mean yield per RM; Sum would add per-acre rates across RMs, which is not a meaningful total.


Yield is a per-acre rate, so adding rates across RMs gives a number with no physical meaning. 📗 Answer workbook — the source data on one tab and a real PivotTable on another. Open it in Excel and the field list is live, so you can drag the fields around and see how the grid changes.





Question 99
Using the Saskatchewan RM Crop Yields dataset (long file).
(a) Build a PivotTable with Crop on Rows and Yield as Average (bu/ac) filtered to 2021 (the low year).
(b) Rank the crops for 2021.
(c) In 2023, Oats is the top-ranked crop by yield. Compare your 2021 (drought-year) ranking to that: does the drought change which crop is on top, or does it scale all crops down together while keeping a similar order?
(d) Explain what it tells you if the ranking of crops stays similar even when every crop’s yield falls.
(e) State, in one sentence, the difference between the level of yields changing and the ranking of crops changing.


Answer



Crop on Rows, Yield Average, 2021.


Oats > Barley > Spring Wheat > Peas > Canola > Durum > Flax (all lower than 2023).


The top crop (Oats) is unchanged; the drought lowered every crop but kept a similar order.


It means the drought scaled all crops down together without changing their relative standing.


The level is how high the yields are; the ranking is their order — a bad year can drop the level while leaving the order intact. 📗 Answer workbook — the source data on one tab and a real PivotTable on another. Open it in Excel and the field list is live, so you can drag the fields around and see how the grid changes.





Question 100
Using the Saskatchewan RM Crop Yields dataset (long file).
(a) Build a PivotTable with Year on Rows and Yield as Average for Canola only, and use it to create a PivotChart (line).
(b) Describe the overall direction of the line and identify the year with the sharpest single-year drop.
(c) Explain the advantage of a PivotChart over a static chart when the underlying PivotTable filters change.
(d) Explain why building the by-year average in a PivotTable first is easier than computing 36 yearly averages by hand.
(e) State, in one sentence, how PivotTables and charts work together to summarise a large dataset.


Answer



PivotChart line of canola average by year.


Rising overall; the sharpest single-year drop is into 2021 (from ~38 to ~22 bu/ac). (The lowest level is 2002 at ~16; here the question asks for the sharpest drop.)


A PivotChart updates automatically when you change the PivotTable’s filters or fields.


The PivotTable computes every year’s average in one step, instead of writing an AVERAGEIF per year.


The PivotTable aggregates the raw rows into a summary, and the chart renders that summary visually. 📗 Answer workbook — the source data on one tab and a real PivotTable on another. Open it in Excel and the field list is live, so you can drag the fields around and see how the grid changes.

Questions 81–90 · Manitoba Wheat Variety

Question 101
Using the Manitoba Wheat Variety dataset.
(a) Build a PivotTable of average reported yield by variety (Variety on Rows, Yield_bu_ac as Average), and add a Count of the rows behind each average.
(b) Identify the variety with the highest average, and the variety that is most widely reported (highest count).
(c) Explain why “highest average” and “most widely reported” can be two different varieties.
(d) Say which of the two you would trust more as a summary, and justify it with the count.
(e) Explain why filtering to varieties with at least 30 reports gives a more trustworthy ranking than including every variety.


Answer



Variety on Rows; Yield Average + Count.


Highest average (unfiltered) ≈ AAC WESTKING (~79) — but on only ~17 reports; most-reported ≈ AAC BRANDON (BW 932) (~519 reports, mean ~60). (Among well-reported varieties with ≥30 reports, SY MANNESS ~72 is the top.)


A variety reported on very few sites can post a high average without being widely reported.


The widely-reported average (AAC Brandon, n≈519) is more trustworthy than a high average on ~17 reports.


Averages from a handful of reports are noisy and can top the list by chance (AAC WESTKING on ~17); a ≥30 threshold keeps only well-supported estimates. 📗 Answer workbook — the source data on one tab and a real PivotTable on another. Open it in Excel and the field list is live, so you can drag the fields around and see how the grid changes.





Question 102
Using the Manitoba Wheat Variety dataset.
(a) Build a PivotTable with Variety on Rows and Year on Columns (Yield as Average) for a few common varieties including AAC BRANDON (BW 932).
(b) Identify AAC Brandon’s weakest year, and describe the size of the dip.
(c) Read across the other varieties’ rows for that same year. Do they dip too?
(d) Explain what it means that several varieties share their weakest year.
(e) Explain how reading the same variety across years isolates the year effect from the variety.


Answer



Variety × Year grid.


AAC Brandon’s 2021 (~49) is well below its ~62–66 in other years.


Yes — other varieties (e.g. Starbuck ~51 in 2021) dip in the same year.


A shared weak year across varieties points to a common year effect rather than a variety fault.


With the variety fixed, year-to-year changes cannot be due to variety, so they reflect the year’s conditions. 📗 Answer workbook — the source data on one tab and a real PivotTable on another. Open it in Excel and the field list is live, so you can drag the fields around and see how the grid changes.





Question 103
Using the Manitoba Wheat Variety dataset.
(a) Build a PivotTable of the count of reported rows by variety (Variety on Rows, Yield as Count).
(b) Identify the three most-reported varieties.
(c) Explain what this count-based PivotTable tells you that an average-yield PivotTable does not.
(d) Explain why you would filter out varieties with very low counts before ranking varieties by average yield.
(e) State, in one sentence, why a count PivotTable is a good first step before comparing variety averages.


Answer



Variety on Rows, Yield → Count.


AAC Brandon (~519), AAC Starbuck (~374), AAC Wheatland (~219).


It shows how much data backs each variety — coverage — not how well each yielded.


Low-count varieties have unstable averages that can distort a ranking.


Knowing the counts first tells you which variety averages are well-supported enough to compare. 📗 Answer workbook — the source data on one tab and a real PivotTable on another. Open it in Excel and the field list is live, so you can drag the fields around and see how the grid changes.





Question 104
Using the Manitoba Wheat Variety dataset.
(a) Build a PivotTable with Year on Rows and Yield as Average (all reported rows), 2020–2025.
(b) Identify the lowest and highest years.
(c) Describe the overall movement of the yearly averages across the six years.
(d) Explain why the yearly average can be affected by which varieties were reported that year, and how a Count column would help you check.
(e) State, in one sentence, why adding a Count column to a by-year PivotTable improves your interpretation.


Answer



Year on Rows, Yield Average.


Lowest 2021 (~49.6), highest 2025 (~68.0).


A dip in 2021 then a steady climb to 2025.


If the mix of reported varieties changes yearly, the average shifts partly for that reason; a Count column shows how many rows (and which years) are thin.


The Count shows how much data supports each year’s average, flagging years to interpret cautiously. 📗 Answer workbook — the source data on one tab and a real PivotTable on another. Open it in Excel and the field list is live, so you can drag the fields around and see how the grid changes.





Question 105
Using the Manitoba Wheat Variety dataset.
(a) Build a PivotTable with Municipality on Rows and Yield as Average (all reported rows) for one year (e.g. 2023).
(b) Identify the highest- and lowest-average municipalities that year.
(c) Explain why a municipality with only one or two reported varieties will have a shaky average, and how a Count column reveals that.
(d) Explain why comparing municipalities is fairer when each rests on several reported varieties.
(e) State, in one sentence, why you would add a Count column before ranking municipalities.


Answer



Municipality on Rows, Yield Average, Year = 2023.


For 2023: highest ALEXANDER ≈84.2 bu/ac, lowest WEST INTERLAKE ≈22.0 — and both rest on a single reported variety, which is exactly why the count column matters. The highest municipality with several reports behind it is ELTON ≈77.5 (5 reports).


One or two varieties give an average from very little data; a Count column exposes those thin municipalities.


With several varieties each, the municipal averages rest on comparable amounts of data.


The Count flags municipalities whose averages come from too few reports to rank reliably. 📗 Answer workbook — the source data on one tab and a real PivotTable on another. Open it in Excel and the field list is live, so you can drag the fields around and see how the grid changes.





Question 106
Using the Manitoba Wheat Variety dataset.
(a) Build a PivotTable with Variety on Rows and Yield as Average, filtered to a single year (e.g. 2025), and add Count.
(b) Rank the varieties for that year (among those with several reports).
(c) Across all years, SY MANNESS is the top-averaging variety (among those with many reports). Compare your single-year ranking to that all-years picture — does the same variety lead, and why can a variety’s rank shift from one year to the next?
(d) Name one thing other than genetics that could move a variety’s rank between years, and explain how averaging across years reduces its effect.
(e) State, in one sentence, why an all-years variety ranking is generally more stable than a one-year ranking.


Answer



Variety on Rows, Yield Average + Count, Year = 2025.


Rank the well-reported varieties for 2025.


Compare to the all-years order; expect broad agreement with some movement.


Where a variety happens to be grown – soil, moisture, the mix of municipalities reporting it in a given year – moves its average independently of the genetics. Averaging over many years and places lets those site effects cancel out rather than deciding the ranking.


Averaging over many years smooths out any one year’s quirks, giving a steadier ranking. 📗 Answer workbook — the source data on one tab and a real PivotTable on another. Open it in Excel and the field list is live, so you can drag the fields around and see how the grid changes.





Question 107
Using the Manitoba Wheat Variety dataset.
(a) Build a PivotTable with Variety on Rows and both Average and Count of Yield, for the whole dataset.
(b) Filter (or sort) to show only varieties with at least 30 reports.
(c) Among those, identify the highest and lowest average.
(d) Explain why applying the ≥30 filter changes which variety appears “best” compared with an unfiltered ranking.
(e) State, in one sentence, why a minimum-count filter is a form of quality control on a ranking.


Answer



Variety on Rows, Yield Average + Count.


Keep varieties with Count ≥ 30.


Highest ≈ SY MANNESS (~72); lowest among the well-reported ≈ AAC Tisdale/Redberry (~54).


Without the filter, a variety with 1–2 lucky reports could top the list; the filter removes those unreliable entries.


It ensures every ranked average rests on enough data to be trusted. 📗 Answer workbook — the source data on one tab and a real PivotTable on another. Open it in Excel and the field list is live, so you can drag the fields around and see how the grid changes.





Question 108
Using the Manitoba Wheat Variety dataset.
(a) Build a PivotTable with Year on Rows and Variety on Columns (Yield as Average) for two varieties (e.g. AAC Brandon and AAC Starbuck).
(b) For each year, note which variety yielded higher.
(c) State whether one variety beats the other in every year, or whether the lead changes.
(d) Explain how this grid separates a consistent variety advantage from a year-specific one.
(e) State, in one sentence, why comparing two varieties across many years is more convincing than comparing them in a single year.


Answer



Year × Variety grid for the two varieties.


Compare the two columns each year (Starbuck is generally higher).


Starbuck leads in most/all years here — a consistent edge, not a one-year fluke.


A lead that holds every year is a genuine variety difference; a lead in only one year could be that year’s conditions.


A consistent multi-year lead rules out chance and single-year effects far better than one comparison. 📗 Answer workbook — the source data on one tab and a real PivotTable on another. Open it in Excel and the field list is live, so you can drag the fields around and see how the grid changes.





Question 109
Using the Manitoba Wheat Variety dataset.
(a) Build a PivotTable of average yield by variety, filter to varieties with at least 30 reports, and turn the highest-averaging ones into a bar PivotChart (ranked by average yield), titled with labelled axes.
(b) Identify the tallest and shortest bars.
(c) Explain what the bar chart shows well and what it hides (compared to also seeing each variety’s Count and spread).
(d) Explain why the bars should start at zero.
(e) State, in one sentence, how a PivotChart keeps the chart in sync with the PivotTable.


Answer



Bar PivotChart of variety averages (≥30 reports), ranked, titled/labelled.


Tallest ≈ SY MANNESS (~72, the highest average among well-reported varieties); shortest among these ≈ AAC Tisdale/Redberry (~54).


It shows the averages clearly but hides how many reports back each and how spread each variety is.


A zero baseline keeps bar heights proportional; a truncated axis exaggerates small gaps.


A PivotChart redraws automatically whenever the PivotTable’s fields or filters change. 📗 Answer workbook — the source data on one tab and a real PivotTable on another. Open it in Excel and the field list is live, so you can drag the fields around and see how the grid changes.





Question 110
Using the Manitoba Wheat Variety dataset.
(a) Build a PivotTable that counts reported vs suppressed rows by variety (Variety on Rows, Reported on Columns, Municipality as Count). Count Municipality rather than Yield_bu_ac: suppressed rows have a blank yield, so counting the yield column would leave the suppressed side of the table empty.
(b) Pick one variety and read off how many of its rows are reported vs suppressed.
(c) Explain what a high suppressed count for a variety tells you about how its data appears in this dataset.
(d) Explain why this reported-vs-suppressed PivotTable is impossible to build if you first delete all suppressed rows.
(e) State, in one sentence, why keeping the suppressed rows (with a flag) makes the dataset more informative.


Answer



Variety on Rows, Reported on Columns, Count of Municipality. Counting Yield_bu_ac instead returns nothing in the FALSE column, because that is exactly the value being suppressed.


Report the TRUE/FALSE split for your chosen variety (e.g. AAC BRANDON (BW 932): 519 TRUE, 51 FALSE).


A high suppressed count means the variety appears in many places but with yields often withheld.


Deleting suppressed rows removes the FALSE column entirely, so the split cannot be shown.


The flagged suppressed rows let you measure coverage and withholding, not just reported yields. 📗 Answer workbook — the source data on one tab and a real PivotTable on another. Open it in Excel and the field list is live, so you can drag the fields around and see how the grid changes.

title: Module 1 — Full Test Bank
text:
Questions 91–100 · Canada Field Crops

Question 111
Using the Canada Field Crops dataset.
(a) Build a PivotTable of average canola yield by province for 2023 (Province on Rows, Yield as Average, Year filtered to 2023). Rank the provinces.
(b) Identify the top-ranked province and Saskatchewan’s rank.
(c) Explain what this pivot does and does not establish about which province is the more important canola province.
(d) Add Seeded_acres as a second value (Sum). Describe how looking at yield and acreage together changes the story.
(e) State the general lesson about distinguishing “yield per acre” from “total production.”


Answer



Ranking by average yield, 2023: Ontario 53.4, New Brunswick 45.6, Manitoba 44.6, Quebec 40.9, Alberta 40.1, Saskatchewan 37.4, BC 35.1.


Ontario ranks top; Saskatchewan is near the bottom on yield per acre.


The pivot ranks yield per acre; it does not establish importance/output.


Saskatchewan seeds ~12.4M acres vs Ontario’s ~45,100 — SK produces vastly more canola overall despite lower yield.


High yield per acre ≠ high total production; you need acreage to judge importance. 📗 Answer workbook — the source data on one tab and a real PivotTable on another. Open it in Excel and the field list is live, so you can drag the fields around and see how the grid changes.





Question 112
Using the Canada Field Crops dataset.
(a) Build a PivotTable with Province on Rows and Year on Columns (canola Yield as Average).
(b) Reading across Saskatchewan’s row, identify its weakest year and describe the gap to a normal year.
(c) Reading down the 2021 column, describe what you notice across provinces.
(d) Explain how this grid lets you tell whether 2021 was a local Saskatchewan problem or a broader one.
(e) State your conclusion about 2021 and the evidence in the grid that supports it.


Answer



Province × Year grid of average canola yield.


Saskatchewan’s 2021 is well below its other years.


Several provinces are low in 2021, not just Saskatchewan.


If the whole 2021 column is low, the cause is broad; if only SK’s cell is low, it’s local.


2021 was a broad, multi-province low year — several provinces dip together in that column. 📗 Answer workbook — the source data on one tab and a real PivotTable on another. Open it in Excel and the field list is live, so you can drag the fields around and see how the grid changes.





Question 113
Using the Canada Field Crops dataset.
(a) Build a PivotTable of total canola seeded acres by province for 2023 (Province on Rows, Seeded_acres as Sum, Year = 2023). Rank the provinces.
(b) Identify the province with the most seeded acres and its rough share of the national total.
(c) By yield per acre, Ontario leads canola. Does the same province lead this seeded-acres ranking? Explain how a province can lead one but not the other.
(d) Multiply each province’s seeded acres by its yield to get approximate production. Explain what that column shows that neither acres nor yield shows alone.
(e) State, in one sentence, why “which province grows the most canola” is answered by acres (or production), not by yield.


Answer



Seeded acres 2023: SK ≈12.4M, AB ≈6.36M, MB ≈3.13M, then far smaller (BC ~109k, ON ~45k, QC ~39k, NB ~1.6k).


Saskatchewan — over half the national canola acreage.


No — SK leads acres but ranks low on yield per acre (Ontario led yield).


Saskatchewan ≈464 million bu, Alberta ≈255 million, Manitoba ≈140 million, British Columbia ≈3.8 million. Production combines both: Ontario’s leading yield sits on so few acres that it never appears near the top, while Saskatchewan’s middling yield over 12.4 million acres dominates. Neither column alone tells you where the canola actually comes from.


“Grows the most” is about scale (acres/production), which yield per acre does not measure. 📗 Answer workbook — the source data on one tab and a real PivotTable on another. Open it in Excel and the field list is live, so you can drag the fields around and see how the grid changes.





Question 114
Using the Canada Field Crops dataset.
(a) Build a PivotTable with Crop on Rows and average Yield across all provinces and years (Yield as Average).
(b) Rank the crops nationally.
(c) Identify the top crop and explain why its high average does not, by itself, tell you it is the most-grown crop.
(d) Explain what additional field you would pivot on (Sum) to judge how much of each crop is grown.
(e) State, in one sentence, why a by-crop yield pivot and a by-crop acres pivot answer different questions.


Answer



Crop on Rows, Yield Average.


Corn for grain highest (~136), then Oats (~79), Barley (~64) … down to Flax (~26).


Corn yields the most per acre, but a high per-acre yield says nothing about how many acres of corn are grown.


Pivot Seeded_acres as Sum by crop to see how much of each is planted.


The yield pivot ranks per-acre productivity; the acres pivot ranks scale — different questions. 📗 Answer workbook — the source data on one tab and a real PivotTable on another. Open it in Excel and the field list is live, so you can drag the fields around and see how the grid changes.





Question 115
Using the Canada Field Crops dataset.
(a) Build a PivotTable of average canola yield by province across all years (Province on Rows, Yield as Average).
(b) Rank the provinces by average canola yield. In the 2023-only ranking, Ontario is highest and Saskatchewan sits near the bottom on yield per acre — is your all-years order similar, and why might a single year differ from the long-run ranking?
(c) State whether the top province is the same in both.
(d) Identify one province whose rank moves most between the two, and say what you would look at next to decide whether that move is real or noise.
(e) State, in one sentence, when you would use the all-years provincial ranking rather than one year’s.


Answer



All-years averages: Ontario 46.7, NB 44.0, MB 41.5, QC 41.4, PEI 40.7, AB 40.1, SK 39.1, BC 35.5.


Similar order to 2023, with small shuffles in the middle.


Yes — Ontario tops both.


Name the province that shifts most between the two rankings, then check how many years it reports and how far apart its individual yearly values sit. A province with few reports, or with widely scattered ones, can move on noise; a consistent one moving is more likely a real change.


Use the all-years ranking for a stable, typical comparison rather than one year’s snapshot. 📗 Answer workbook — the source data on one tab and a real PivotTable on another. Open it in Excel and the field list is live, so you can drag the fields around and see how the grid changes.





Question 116
Using the Canada Field Crops dataset.
(a) Build a PivotTable with Year on Rows and Sum of canola Seeded_acres (all provinces), 2015–2025.
(b) Describe the overall trend in national canola seeded acres over the period.
(c) Explain why summing seeded acres across provinces is a valid total, unlike summing yields.
(d) Explain why you set the aggregation to Sum here, not Average.
(e) State, in one sentence, what this by-year acres total tells you that a by-year yield average would not.


Answer



Year on Rows, Seeded_acres as Sum.


Canola acres sit between roughly 20.8 and 23.0 million all decade — up to a 2017 peak of ≈23.0M, then drifting around 21–22M. The striking feature is how flat it is.


Acres add up (extensive), so the national total is meaningful; yields are per-acre rates and cannot be summed.


Sum gives the national total acreage; Average would give a per-province average acreage, a different quantity.


It shows the crop’s changing national footprint (how much land), not how well it yielded. 📗 Answer workbook — the source data on one tab and a real PivotTable on another. Open it in Excel and the field list is live, so you can drag the fields around and see how the grid changes.





Question 117
Using the Canada Field Crops dataset.
(a) Build a PivotTable with Province on Rows and Sum of Seeded_acres for spring wheat in 2023.
(b) Rank the provinces by seeded acres.
(c) Add average Yield as a second value. Identify a province that ranks high on acres but not on yield (or vice versa).
(d) Explain how showing acres and yield side by side tells a fuller story than either alone.
(e) State, in one sentence, why a province’s contribution to national production depends on both its acres and its yield.


Answer



Province on Rows, Seeded_acres as Sum, spring wheat 2023.


Prairie provinces (SK, then AB, MB) lead seeded acres.


Report a province high on one measure but not the other from your pivot.


Acres show scale, yield shows per-acre performance; together they explain which provinces drive production.


Production = yield × acres, so a province needs both to contribute heavily to the national total. 📗 Answer workbook — the source data on one tab and a real PivotTable on another. Open it in Excel and the field list is live, so you can drag the fields around and see how the grid changes.





Question 118
Using the Canada Field Crops dataset.
(a) Build a PivotTable with Crop on Rows and Count of non-blank Yield values (Yield as Count), all provinces and years.
(b) Identify a crop with a high count and one with a low count.
(c) Explain what a low count tells you about how many province-years reported that crop.
(d) Explain why a crop’s low count means its national average rests on fewer province-years.
(e) State, in one sentence, why a Count PivotTable is a useful check before trusting a crop’s national average.


Answer



Crop on Rows, Yield → Count.


Widely grown crops (canola, barley, spring wheat) have high counts; durum and flax have lower counts.


A low count means few province-years reported that crop — it is grown in fewer places.


Fewer reporting province-years means the national average is built from less data and covers less of the country.


The count shows how broadly a crop is reported, so you know how far its national average really extends. 📗 Answer workbook — the source data on one tab and a real PivotTable on another. Open it in Excel and the field list is live, so you can drag the fields around and see how the grid changes.





Question 119
Using the Canada Field Crops dataset.
(a) Build a PivotTable with Province on Rows and Year on Columns (Sum of canola Seeded_acres).
(b) Reading across Saskatchewan’s row, describe how its canola acreage changed over the years.
(c) Reading down a recent year’s column, confirm which province plants the most canola.
(d) Explain why a Province × Year acres grid is a good way to see both who grows the most and how their acreage is changing.
(e) State, in one sentence, why Sum (not Average) is the correct aggregation for a seeded-acres grid.


Answer



Province × Year grid, Seeded_acres as Sum.


Describe SK’s canola acreage path across the years from your grid.


Saskatchewan plants the most canola in recent years (~12M+ acres).


Rows show each province’s trend; columns show who leads in a given year — the grid shows both at once.


Acres are additive totals, so Sum gives each province-year’s true acreage; Average would misrepresent it. 📗 Answer workbook — the source data on one tab and a real PivotTable on another. Open it in Excel and the field list is live, so you can drag the fields around and see how the grid changes.





Question 120
Using the Canada Field Crops dataset.
(a) Build a PivotTable of average canola yield by province (all years) and turn it into a bar PivotChart, titled with labelled axes.
(b) Identify the highest and lowest province bars.
(c) Explain why this yield chart alone could mislead someone into thinking the top-bar province is Canada’s biggest canola producer.
(d) Describe the second chart (a bar chart of Sum of seeded acres by province) you would place beside it to complete the story.
(e) State, in one sentence, the overall lesson this pair of charts teaches about yield versus production.


Answer



Bar PivotChart of provincial canola yield averages, titled/labelled.


Highest ≈ Ontario; lowest ≈ British Columbia.


A viewer might assume the highest-yield province grows the most canola, but yield per acre is not production.


A bar chart of Sum of seeded acres by province, which would show Saskatchewan towering over the rest.


The province that yields the most per acre is not the one that produces the most canola — you need both yield and acres. 📗 Answer workbook — the source data on one tab and a real PivotTable on another. Open it in Excel and the field list is live, so you can drag the fields around and see how the grid changes.

title: Module 2 — Test Bank
text:
Section 1 — R Basics
The data. Three datasets, six files, all in your project’s data/ folder:
Saskatchewan RM crop yields – average yields in every Saskatchewan Rural Municipality, one row per RM-year(-crop), columns Year, RM, Crop, Yield, Unit:
Manitoba wheat variety yields – MASC’s variety-level spring wheat yields, one row per municipality-variety-year, 2020–2025, columns Year, Municipality, Variety, Farms, Acres, Yield_bu_ac, Reported. Where too few farms grew a variety, the row is suppressed for privacy: Reported is FALSE and the numeric columns are missing.
Canada field crops – Statistics Canada’s provincial estimates, one row per province-crop-year, 2015–2025, columns Year, Province, Crop, Seeded_acres, Yield_bu_ac:
Grading model. 20% for script presentation – a header block, comments in the style of the module, clearly labelled question sections, and a script that runs from top to bottom in a fresh session. The remaining 80% is split evenly across the four questions, and evenly across the parts within each question. Parts are marked on follow-through: if an early part is wrong but the later parts are correctly worked from your own earlier answer, the later parts still earn full marks. Where a part asks for a sentence, write it as a comment in your script.
These questions are about the building blocks: objects, vectors, data frames, and functions. No data file is needed – the numbers are in the question. Answer in the Section 1 block of your script, with sentence answers written as comments.

title: Module 2 — Test Bank
text:
Questions 31–40 · Saskatchewan RM Canola
These questions use the canola-only file, rm_canola_yields_1990_2025.csv, in your project’s data/ folder.

Question 31
(a) In a comment at the top of your script, sketch your project’s folder layout (the subfolders and where the csv sits).
(b) Load the tidyverse and read the canola file into an object called rm_canola, using a relative path.
(c) Report the number of rows, the number of columns, and the column names using functions.
(d) In a comment: why will your read_csv() line work on the grader’s computer, when a full path starting C:/Users/... would not?


Answer

library(tidyverse)
rm_canola <- read_csv("data/rm_canola_yields_1990_2025.csv")
nrow(rm_canola); ncol(rm_canola); names(rm_canola)


10,039 rows, 5 columns: Year, RM, Crop, Yield, Unit.


The path is relative to the project folder, and the grader opens the same self-contained folder – so data/... exists on their machine too. An absolute path names one particular computer’s user and folder layout.





Question 32
A classmate’s script reads the data like this:
rm_canola <- read_csv("C:\\Users\\jordan\\Desktop\\stats stuff\\rm_canola_yields_1990_2025.csv")
It runs on their laptop and fails on everyone else’s.
(a) In a comment: give two separate problems with this line (one about where the path points, one about the backslashes).
(b) Rewrite the line the way the module recommends, assuming the csv is in the project’s data/ folder.
(c) In a comment: the classmate asks “but with your short path, how does R know where to start looking?” Answer in one sentence.
(d) Your fixed line could itself fail with Error: 'data/rm_canola_yields_1990_2025.csv' does not exist in current working directory (...). In a comment: what is the first thing to check?


Answer



The absolute path names one specific machine (user jordan, a Desktop folder), so it exists nowhere else; and backslashes mean something special inside an R string – paths in R use forward slashes even on Windows.


rm_canola <- read_csv("data/rm_canola_yields_1990_2025.csv").


Opening the project folder in Positron (File → Open Folder…) makes that folder R’s starting point, so relative paths begin from it.


That the folder opened in Positron is the project folder – the one that contains data/ with the csv inside. If some other folder is open, the relative path starts from the wrong place.





Question 33
You organized the course as one big folder and opened AREC_261/ in Positron:
AREC_261/
  module_2/
    data/
      rm_canola_yields_1990_2025.csv
    code/
  README.md
(a) Write the read_csv() line that works with this setup.
(b) In a comment: your line from (a) stops working after you re-organize and open module_2/ itself in Positron. Why, and what does the path become?
(c) In a comment: starting from the opened AREC_261/ folder, trace how R follows your path from (a) to the file, one folder at a time.


Answer



rm_canola <- read_csv("module_2/data/rm_canola_yields_1990_2025.csv").


The starting point changed: relative paths begin at the folder you opened. With module_2/ open, the path is data/rm_canola_yields_1990_2025.csv.


From AREC_261, R goes into module_2, then into data, and finds rm_canola_yields_1990_2025.csv – each / steps into a subfolder.





Question 34
(a) Run glimpse() on rm_canola. In a comment: which columns are text (<chr>) and which are numeric (<dbl>)?
(b) When read_csv() ran, it printed a note about the file. In a comment: what did that note report, and why does the module say to read it every time?
(c) Year came in as numeric (<dbl>). In a comment: which type of value is each of 2024 and "2024"? Why do we want a column we will compute with stored as numbers rather than as text?


Answer



Crop and Unit are <chr>; Year, RM, and Yield are <dbl>.


The row and column counts and its guess at each column’s type (here chr (2) and dbl (3)). R guesses well but not perfectly, so the note is the first check that the file read the way you expect.


2024 is numeric; "2024" is character (text). Numbers stored as text stop behaving like numbers – you cannot do arithmetic with them, and sorting turns alphabetical – so a column you will compute with should show <dbl>, not <chr>.





Question 35
(a) Run summary(rm_canola). From its output, report the minimum, median, and maximum of Yield, and the first and last Year.
(b) In a comment: work through the module’s inspection questions for this file. Are the yields in a plausible range for canola in bu/ac? Are the years what the file name promises? Are there missing values?
(c) The minimum is below 2 bu/ac. In a comment: is a canola yield that low necessarily a data error? What kind of year could produce it?


Answer



Yield: min 1.9, median 26.9, max 61. Years 1990 to 2025.


Yes – everything sits between about 2 and 61 bu/ac, sensible for canola; the years run 1990–2025 as advertised; and summary() prints an NA's count only when a column has missing values – no such line appears, so there are none.


Not necessarily – an RM average that low is what a severe drought or a widespread crop failure looks like. Extreme is not the same as wrong; it is a value to investigate, not delete.





Question 36
(a) Compute the mean, median, standard deviation, and variance of rm_canola$Yield.
(b) Compute the 90th percentile of Yield.
(c) The mean sits a little above the median. In a comment: using Module 1’s language about means and medians, what does that direction of gap suggest about the shape of canola yields?


Answer

mean(rm_canola$Yield)
median(rm_canola$Yield)
sd(rm_canola$Yield)
var(rm_canola$Yield)
quantile(rm_canola$Yield, 0.9)


Mean 28.29, median 26.9, sd 10.06, variance 101.21 (the sd squared, in squared units).


90th percentile 42.5.


A mean above the median suggests mild right skew: the very best RM-years pull the mean up more than the worst years pull it down.





Question 37
Open rm_canola_yields_1990_2025.csv in Positron’s data viewer (click the file in the Explorer pane).
(a) In a comment: according to the viewer’s summary panel, does any column have missing values?
(b) In a comment: expand the Yield column’s summary. Describe the shape of its histogram in one phrase, and say whether it matches your mean-versus-median reading from Question 36.
(c) A classmate says “the file is open in the viewer, so it’s loaded into R.” In a comment: correct them, and say what actually loads it.


Answer



No – the summary panel shows 0% missing for every column.


A single hump around the mid-20s with a longer tail to the right – consistent with the mean sitting a little above the median.


The viewer is Positron showing you the file; nothing exists in R until read_csv() runs and the result is assigned to an object.





Question 38
(a) Compute the 25th and 75th percentiles of Yield in a single quantile() call.
(b) Compute the interquartile range twice: once with IQR(), once by subtracting your two percentiles.
(c) In a comment: say what the interquartile range from (b) means in words, for a reader who farms.


Answer

quantile(rm_canola$Yield, c(0.25, 0.75))
IQR(rm_canola$Yield)


25th 21, 75th 35.4.


Both give 14.4.


The middle half of all RM-year canola yields falls between 21 and 35.4 bu/ac – a typical RM in a typical year lands somewhere in that 14-bushel window.





Question 39
A classmate’s fresh R session runs rm_yields <- read_csv("data/rm_yields_1990_2025.csv") and gets:
Error in read_csv(...) : could not find function "read_csv"
(a) In a comment: what is the most likely cause, and what one line fixes it?
(b) In a comment: they object, “but I installed the tidyverse last week!” Explain the difference between installing and loading, and how often each is done.
(c) In a comment: state the quotes rule – where do quotation marks go when installing, and when loading?
(d) The tidyverse is a collection of packages. In comments, name the four core ones from the module and the job each does.


Answer



The package is not loaded in this session; run library(tidyverse) first.


Installing downloads the package onto the computer – once per computer. Loading switches it on – once per script or session. Installation does not carry across sessions as loaded.


Quotes when you install (install.packages("tidyverse")), none when you load (library(tidyverse)).


readr reads data, dplyr manipulates it, tidyr reshapes it, ggplot2 makes graphs.





Question 40
You spot an obviously wrong yield value in the csv. A classmate suggests opening the file in Excel, fixing the cell, and saving. Separately, your download folder contains RM Yields FINAL (2).csv.
(a) In a comment: what is wrong with the classmate’s suggestion, and where should the correction happen instead?
(b) In a comment: give two problems with the file name, and rename it following the module’s two rules.
(c) In a comment: if a date belonged in the file name, how should it be written, and what is the advantage?


Answer



It overwrites the only copy of the raw data and leaves no record of what changed. Keep the file exactly as it arrived and make the correction in the R script, where it leaves a trail.


Spaces and punctuation, and a FINAL (2) tag that will only ever breed a FINAL (3). Something like rm_yields_long.csv.


As YYYY-MM-DD, e.g. 2026-10-08_rm_yields.csv – alphabetical order is then also chronological order.

title: Module 2 — Test Bank
text:
Questions 41–50 · Manitoba Wheat Variety
These questions use mb_wheat_reported_2020_2025.csv – spring wheat yields by variety and municipality, reported observations only.

Question 41
(a) In a comment at the top of your script, sketch your project’s folder layout.
(b) Load the tidyverse and read the file into an object called mb_wheat, using a relative path.
(c) Report the number of rows, the number of columns, and the column names using functions.
(d) In a comment: what does one row of this dataset represent?


Answer

library(tidyverse)
mb_wheat <- read_csv("data/mb_wheat_reported_2020_2025.csv")
nrow(mb_wheat); ncol(mb_wheat); names(mb_wheat)


2,398 rows, 7 columns: Year, Municipality, Variety, Farms, Acres, Yield_bu_ac, Reported.


One wheat variety grown in one municipality in one year – its farm count, acres, and average yield.





Question 42
A classmate’s script reads the data like this:
mb_wheat <- read_csv("/Users/sam/Downloads/mb wheat data.csv")
It works on their laptop and fails on everyone else’s.
(a) In a comment: give two problems – one about where the path points, one about the file’s name and location.
(b) Rewrite the line the way the module recommends, assuming the file was saved as mb_wheat_reported_2020_2025.csv in the project’s data/ folder.
(c) In a comment: your line fails with does not exist in current working directory. What is the first thing to check?


Answer



The absolute path names one machine’s user folder, so it exists nowhere else; and the file is loose in Downloads under a space-filled name instead of renamed and placed in the project’s data/ folder.


mb_wheat <- read_csv("data/mb_wheat_reported_2020_2025.csv").


That the folder opened in Positron is the project folder – the one containing data/. Relative paths start from the opened folder.





Question 43
Your course folder is organized as:
AREC_261/
  module_2/
    data/
      mb_wheat_reported_2020_2025.csv
    code/
  README.md
(a) Write the read_csv() line that works with AREC_261/ open in Positron.
(b) In a comment: what does the path become if you open module_2/ instead?
(c) In a comment: trace how R follows your path from (a) to the file, one folder at a time.


Answer



mb_wheat <- read_csv("module_2/data/mb_wheat_reported_2020_2025.csv").


data/mb_wheat_reported_2020_2025.csv – relative paths begin at the opened folder.


From AREC_261, R steps into module_2, then into data, and finds the csv; each / is one step down.





Question 44
(a) Run glimpse() on mb_wheat. In a comment: which columns are text (<chr>), which numeric (<dbl>), and which logical (<lgl>)?
(b) In a comment: what values does the logical column hold in this file, and why is that no accident? (Look at the file’s name.)
(c) In a comment: Farms holds whole numbers. Would glimpse() showing it as <chr> be a problem, and what would it tell you about the file?


Answer



Municipality and Variety are <chr>; Year, Farms, Acres, Yield_bu_ac are <dbl>; Reported is <lgl>.


All TRUE – this is the reported-only file, with the suppressed (FALSE) rows removed.


Yes – a numeric column arriving as text means some value in it could not be read as a number, and calculations like mean() would fail on it.





Question 45
(a) Run summary(mb_wheat). From its output, report the minimum, median, and maximum of Yield_bu_ac, and the first and last Year.
(b) In a comment: work through the module’s inspection questions. Are the yields in a plausible range for spring wheat? Are there missing values?
(c) The minimum is 4.5 bu/ac. In a comment: is a reported yield that low necessarily an error?


Answer



Yield: min 4.5, median 62.2, max 97.8. Years 2020 to 2025.


Plausible – most values sit tens-of-bushels, sensible for Manitoba wheat; no NA's lines appear, so no missing values in this file.


Not necessarily – a variety on a few drought- or flood-hit fields can genuinely average that low. Extreme is a value to investigate, not delete.





Question 46
(a) Compute the mean, median, standard deviation, and variance of mb_wheat$Yield_bu_ac.
(b) In a comment: the mean sits a little below the median here. In Module 1’s language, what does that direction of gap suggest, and what kind of observations would produce it?
(c) Compute the smallest and largest yields in one range() call.


Answer

mean(mb_wheat$Yield_bu_ac)
median(mb_wheat$Yield_bu_ac)
sd(mb_wheat$Yield_bu_ac)
var(mb_wheat$Yield_bu_ac)
range(mb_wheat$Yield_bu_ac)


Mean 61.16, median 62.2, sd 12.38, variance 153.34.


Mild left skew: unusually low values pull the mean down more than the high values pull it up – a tail of very poor variety-municipality observations mixed in with normal ones.


[1]  4.5 97.8 – range() returns both ends as one vector.





Question 47
Open mb_wheat_reported_2020_2025.csv in Positron’s data viewer.
(a) In a comment: according to the viewer’s summary panel, does any column have missing values?
(b) In a comment: expand Yield_bu_ac. Describe the histogram’s shape in one phrase, and say whether it matches your mean-versus-median reading from Question 46.
(c) A classmate says “it’s open in the viewer, so it’s loaded into R.” In a comment: correct them.


Answer



No – 0% missing in every column of this file.


A single hump around the low 60s with a longer tail stretching left – consistent with the mean sitting below the median.


The viewer is Positron showing the file; nothing exists in R until read_csv() runs and the result is assigned to an object.





Question 48
(a) Compute the 25th and 75th percentiles of Yield_bu_ac in one quantile() call.
(b) Compute the interquartile range twice: with IQR(), and by subtracting your percentiles.
(c) In a comment: say what the IQR means in words, for a reader who farms.


Answer

quantile(mb_wheat$Yield_bu_ac, c(0.25, 0.75))
IQR(mb_wheat$Yield_bu_ac)


25th 53.9, 75th 69.6.


Both give 15.7.


The middle half of variety-municipality yields lands between about 54 and 70 bu/ac – a typical observation falls in that 16-bushel window.





Question 49
A classmate installed the tidyverse last week. Today they restart R, run mb_wheat <- read_csv("data/mb_wheat_reported_2020_2025.csv") as their first line, and get could not find function "read_csv".
(a) In a comment: what happened, and what one line fixes it?
(b) In a comment: how often is installing done, and how often is loading done?
(c) In a comment: state the quotes rule for the two commands.


Answer



Installing survives across sessions but loading does not – each new session starts with no packages loaded. Run library(tidyverse) first.


Install once per computer; load once per script or session.


Quotes when you install (install.packages("tidyverse")), none when you load (library(tidyverse)).





Question 50
You spot what looks like a data-entry slip in the csv, and your download folder contains MB Wheat FINAL final(3).csv.
(a) In a comment: a classmate suggests opening the csv in Excel, typing in a corrected yield, and saving. What is wrong with that, and where should any correction live?
(b) In a comment: give two problems with the file name and rename it following the module’s rules.
(c) In a comment: if you wanted the download date in the name, how would you write it and why?


Answer



It overwrites the only copy of the raw data with an invented value and leaves no record. Raw data stays exactly as it arrived; corrections happen in the R script, where they are visible and reversible.


Spaces plus a FINAL final(3) tag that only breeds a final(4). Something like mb_wheat_yields_2020_2025.csv.


As YYYY-MM-DD (e.g. 2026-10-08_mb_wheat.csv) so alphabetical order is also chronological order.

title: Module 2 — Test Bank
text:
Questions 51–60 · Canada Field Crops
These questions use statcan_spring_wheat_2015_2025.csv – Statistics Canada spring wheat seeded acres and average yield by province.

Question 51
(a) In a comment at the top of your script, sketch your project’s folder layout.
(b) Load the tidyverse and read the file into an object called sw, using a relative path.
(c) Report the number of rows, the number of columns, and the column names using functions.
(d) In a comment: what does one row of this dataset represent?


Answer

library(tidyverse)
sw <- read_csv("data/statcan_spring_wheat_2015_2025.csv")
nrow(sw); ncol(sw); names(sw)


94 rows, 5 columns: Year, Province, Crop, Seeded_acres, Yield_bu_ac.


One province in one year: its spring wheat seeded acres and average yield.





Question 52
A classmate’s script reads the data like this:
sw <- read_csv("C:\\Users\\alex\\Desktop\\statcan spring wheat.csv")
(a) In a comment: give two problems with this line.
(b) Rewrite it the way the module recommends, with the file in the project’s data/ folder under its proper name.
(c) In a comment: the rewritten line still fails on your machine. What is the first thing to check?


Answer



The absolute path names one machine (user alex, a Desktop folder); and backslashes mean something special inside an R string – write forward slashes even on Windows.


sw <- read_csv("data/statcan_spring_wheat_2015_2025.csv").


That the folder opened in Positron is the project folder containing data/ – the relative path starts from whatever folder is open.





Question 53
(a) With AREC_261/ open in Positron and the csv at AREC_261/module_2/data/, write the working read_csv() line.
(b) In a comment: a classmate with the same folders gets does not exist from your exact line. What is different about their session?
(c) In a comment: trace how R follows your path from (a) to the file, one folder at a time.


Answer



sw <- read_csv("module_2/data/statcan_spring_wheat_2015_2025.csv").


They opened a different folder (for example module_2/ itself, or no folder at all) – the relative path starts from the opened folder, so the same line works or fails depending on the starting point, not the code.


From AREC_261, R steps into module_2, then into data, and finds the csv; each / is one step down.





Question 54
(a) Run glimpse() on sw. In a comment: which columns are text and which are numeric?
(b) In a comment: when read_csv() ran, what did its note report for this file?
(c) In a comment: Statistics Canada sometimes publishes a suppressed value as the letter x. If even one Seeded_acres value in the csv were an x, what type would the whole column arrive as, and what would break?


Answer



Province and Crop are <chr>; Year, Seeded_acres, and Yield_bu_ac are <dbl>.


94 rows, 5 columns, and its type guesses: chr (2), dbl (3).


Text – a column takes one type, and one value that cannot be read as a number turns the whole column <chr>. Every calculation on it (mean(), comparisons, sorting by size) would then fail, which is why the types line in glimpse() is worth a glance after every read.





Question 55
(a) Run summary(sw). From its output, report the minimum, median, and maximum of Yield_bu_ac, and the first and last Year.
(b) In a comment: run the module’s inspection questions. Plausible ranges? Missing values? The variables you expected?
(c) Open the csv in Positron’s data viewer and expand Seeded_acres. In a comment: describe its histogram’s shape in one phrase.


Answer



Yield: min 33.7, median 50.9, max 73.9. Years 2015 to 2025.


Yields of 34–74 bu/ac are sensible for provincial spring wheat averages; no NA's lines appear, so nothing is missing; the five expected columns are present.


Almost everything piled near zero with a long tail stretching right – a few prairie-sized values dwarf the rest.





Question 56
(a) Compute the mean, median, and standard deviation of sw$Yield_bu_ac.
(b) In a comment: the mean and median here are nearly equal. What does that suggest about the shape of provincial wheat yields, in Module 1’s language?


Answer

mean(sw$Yield_bu_ac)
median(sw$Yield_bu_ac)
sd(sw$Yield_bu_ac)


Mean 51.32, median 50.9, sd 7.52.


Roughly symmetric – neither tail is pulling the mean away from the median.





Question 57
(a) Compute the mean and the median of sw$Seeded_acres.
(b) The mean is about 2.06 million acres; the median is about 115 thousand. In a comment: that is a gap of nearly twenty to one – what does it tell you, and what feature of Canadian wheat growing produces it?
(c) In a comment: a reporter wants one number for “the typical province’s wheat acreage.” Which of your two numbers do you give them?


Answer

mean(sw$Seeded_acres)
median(sw$Seeded_acres)


Mean 2,063,932; median 114,773.


A mean far above the median flags a few enormous values pulling it up – Saskatchewan and Alberta seed millions of acres while most provinces seed tens of thousands, so the distribution is heavily right-skewed.


The median – the mean describes no actual province, sitting far above the typical one because of the prairie giants.





Question 58
(a) Compute the 25th and 75th percentiles of Yield_bu_ac in one call, and the IQR twice (function, and subtraction).
(b) In a comment: say what the IQR means here in words.


Answer

quantile(sw$Yield_bu_ac, c(0.25, 0.75))
IQR(sw$Yield_bu_ac)


25th 47.3, 75th 56.1; IQR 8.8 both ways.


The middle half of province-year wheat yields falls in a nine-bushel window, from about 47 to 56 bu/ac.





Question 59
A classmate on a brand-new laptop runs:
install.packages(tidyverse)
and gets Error: object 'tidyverse' not found.
(a) In a comment: what rule from the module did they break, and what is the corrected line?
(b) In a comment: after installing correctly, what line still has to appear at the top of the script, and why?
(c) The tidyverse is a collection of packages. In comments, name the four core ones from the module and the job each does.


Answer



The quotes rule – the package name is quoted when installing. Without quotes, R looks for an object called tidyverse and finds none. Corrected: install.packages("tidyverse").


library(tidyverse) – installing puts the package on the computer, but each script or session has to load it before its functions exist.


readr reads data, dplyr manipulates it, tidyr reshapes it, ggplot2 makes graphs.





Question 60
Your download folder contains sk wheat data (new) FINAL.csv.
(a) In a comment: list every violation of the module’s file-naming rules in that name, and rename it properly.
(b) In a comment: why does the module say to save the file into data/ untouched, even before you have looked at it?
(c) In a comment: if you wanted the download date in the name, how would you write it and why?


Answer



Spaces, parentheses, and a FINAL tag standing in for version control. Something like statcan_spring_wheat_2015_2025.csv.


data/ holds raw files exactly as they arrived, so there is always an untouched original to go back to; every change happens in the script, where it leaves a record.


As YYYY-MM-DD (e.g. 2026-10-08_statcan_spring_wheat.csv) so alphabetical order is also chronological order.

title: Module 2 — Test Bank
text:
Questions 61–70 · Saskatchewan RM Crop Yields
These questions use the full eight-crop file: read rm_yields_1990_2025.csv into an object called rm_yields at the start of this block.

Question 61
(a) Filter rm_yields to Canola in 2024, saving the result as canola_2024. How many rows are in the filtered data frame?
(b) From canola_2024, select only the RM and Yield columns, saving the result. Report its column names and its number of columns.
(c) In a comment: after (a) and (b), how many rows does rm_yields itself have, and why?


Answer

canola_2024 <- filter(rm_yields, Crop == "Canola" & Year == 2024)
nrow(canola_2024)
canola_slim <- select(canola_2024, RM, Yield)
names(canola_slim)
ncol(canola_slim)


293 rows.


RM, Yield; 2 columns (still 293 rows).


Still 71,104 – filter() and select() return new data frames and leave the original untouched.





Question 62
(a) Filter to rows where the crop is Oats or Barley, using |, saving the result. How many rows are in the filtered data frame?
(b) Write the same filter using %in% and confirm the row count matches.
(c) Sort your filtered data frame from highest yield to lowest. Which crop, RM, and year hold the top spot, and at what yield?
(d) In a comment: a classmate tried filter(rm_yields, Crop == "Oats" & Crop == "Barley") and got zero rows. Why?


Answer

oats_barley <- filter(rm_yields, Crop == "Oats" | Crop == "Barley")
nrow(oats_barley)
oats_barley2 <- filter(rm_yields, Crop %in% c("Oats", "Barley"))
nrow(oats_barley2)
arrange(oats_barley, desc(Yield))

(a, b) 19,709 rows both ways.

A tie at 165.1 bu/ac: Oats in RM 369 (2025) and Oats in RM 438 (2020) share the maximum, so either is a correct top row.


& requires both conditions true of the same row, and no single row’s crop is both Oats and Barley. “Or” is the right connector.





Question 63
(a) Filter to the Spring Wheat observations of at least 60 bu/ac (all years), using >= and saving the result. How many rows are in the filtered data frame?
(b) Filter again to keep only the 2023 rows of that result. How many rows are in this second data frame?
(c) From your 2023 data frame, select RM and Yield and sort best-first. Which RM tops the list, at what yield?
(d) In a comment: rewrite the condition “yield at least 60 and the crop is not Spring Wheat” using !.


Answer

sw_60 <- filter(rm_yields, Crop == "Spring Wheat" & Yield >= 60)
nrow(sw_60)
sw_60_2023 <- filter(sw_60, Year == 2023)
nrow(sw_60_2023)
sw_best <- select(sw_60_2023, RM, Yield)
arrange(sw_best, desc(Yield))


434 rows. (b) 53 rows.


RM 187, at 74.7 bu/ac.


filter(rm_yields, Yield >= 60 & !Crop == "Spring Wheat").





Question 64
(a) Make a version of the data with only Year, RM, Crop, and Yield – once by naming what you keep, once by dropping what you don’t want – saving each, and confirm the two have the same column names. Then make a third version keeping the adjacent-column range Year:Crop, and report its column names.
(b) Rename Yield to yield_per_acre in the full data, saving the result, and show the new column names.
(c) Filter your renamed data frame to Peas in 2025. How many rows are in the filtered data frame?


Answer

kept    <- select(rm_yields, Year, RM, Crop, Yield)
dropped <- select(rm_yields, -Unit)
names(kept)
names(dropped)
ranged  <- select(rm_yields, Year:Crop)
names(ranged)
renamed <- rename(rm_yields, yield_per_acre = Yield)
names(renamed)
peas_2025 <- filter(renamed, Crop == "Peas" & Year == 2025)
nrow(peas_2025)


Identical: Year, RM, Crop, Yield both ways; the range version keeps Year, RM, Crop.


Year, RM, Crop, yield_per_acre, Unit.


285 rows.





Question 65
Lentil yields are in pounds per acre; one pound per acre is about 1.12 kg per hectare.
(a) Filter to the lentil rows, saving as lentils. How many rows are in the filtered data frame?
(b) Use mutate() to add a yield_kg_ha column to lentils, saving the result back to lentils.
(c) Compute the mean of the new column, and the mean of the original Yield column, and check the ratio is the conversion factor.


Answer

lentils <- filter(rm_yields, Crop == "Lentils")
nrow(lentils)
lentils <- mutate(lentils, yield_kg_ha = Yield * 1.12)
mean(lentils$yield_kg_ha)
mean(lentils$Yield)


6,338 rows.


Mean 1,353.4 kg/ha vs 1,208.39 lb/ac – and 1353.4 / 1208.39 ≈ 1.12.





Question 66
(a) Filter to Canola in 2024, then in one mutate() call add two columns: yield_t_ha (multiply by 0.0560) and yield_kg_ha (multiply by 56.0). Save each step.
(b) Compute the mean of each new column.
(c) Sort by yield_t_ha, best first. Which RM tops the table, and at what yield in t/ha?
(d) In a comment: without running anything, what is the mean of yield_kg_ha divided by the mean of yield_t_ha, and why?


Answer

canola_2024 <- filter(rm_yields, Crop == "Canola" & Year == 2024)
canola_2024 <- mutate(canola_2024,
                      yield_t_ha  = Yield * 0.0560,
                      yield_kg_ha = Yield * 56.0)
mean(canola_2024$yield_t_ha)
mean(canola_2024$yield_kg_ha)
arrange(canola_2024, desc(yield_t_ha))


1.76 t/ha and 1,764.11 kg/ha.


RM 493, at 2.57 t/ha.


1,000 – both columns are the same yields scaled by constants, and 56.0 / 0.0560 = 1000 (a tonne is 1,000 kg).





Question 67
(a) Filter to Flax in 2025, saving as flax_2025. How many rows are in the filtered data frame?
(b) Sort it from highest yield to lowest, and report the RM and yield in the top row.
(c) Sort it from lowest to highest instead. What changes in the code?
(d) In a comment: after (b) and (c), is flax_2025 itself now sorted? Why or why not?


Answer

flax_2025 <- filter(rm_yields, Crop == "Flax" & Year == 2025)
nrow(flax_2025)
arrange(flax_2025, desc(Yield))
arrange(flax_2025, Yield)


195 rows.


RM 381 at 45.5 bu/ac.


Drop the desc().


No – neither sorted result was assigned, so both were displayed and discarded; flax_2025 is unchanged.





Question 68
A script contains, in order:
filter(rm_yields, Crop == "Peas")
peas <- filter(rm_yields, Crop == "Peas")
(a) In a comment: what does each line do, and what appears in the console after each?
(b) Report nrow(peas) and nrow(rm_yields).
(c) In a comment: connect this to the same distinction you met with x * 3 in the console back in Section 1.


Answer



Line 1 computes the pea rows and prints them – nothing is saved. Line 2 computes the same thing and saves it as peas, printing nothing.


nrow(peas) is 9,270; nrow(rm_yields) is still 71,104.


It is displaying versus saving again: an expression’s result appears in the console and vanishes unless assigned to an object.





Question 69
(a) Filter to Canola in RM 232 (all years), saving the result. How many rows are in the filtered data frame?
(b) From that object, select only Year and Yield, saving again.
(c) Sort it so the best year is on top. Which year was it, and what was the yield?


Answer

canola_232 <- filter(rm_yields, Crop == "Canola" & RM == 232)
nrow(canola_232)
canola_232 <- select(canola_232, Year, Yield)
arrange(canola_232, desc(Yield))


31 rows (some years are missing – the crop was not grown or reported in that RM every year).


2016, at 43.9 bu/ac.





Question 70
(a) Using head(), display the first six rows of rm_yields.
(b) Sort the data by Yield in descending order into a new object, select its Crop, Yield, and Unit columns into another, and display the first six rows of that (leaving rm_yields unchanged throughout).
(c) In a comment: every row in (b) is the same crop. Which one, why those rows, and what would you check before comparing their values with the other crops?
(d) Now sort by Crop first and by descending Yield within each crop, into a new object, and display its first six rows. Which crop fills them, and why that crop?


Answer

head(rm_yields)
sorted <- arrange(rm_yields, desc(Yield))
top_cols <- select(sorted, Crop, Yield, Unit)
head(top_cols)
by_crop <- arrange(rm_yields, Crop, desc(Yield))
head(by_crop)

(b, c) All lentils – their yields are recorded in pounds per acre, so they dominate the top of any sort on Yield. Before comparing across crops you would check the Unit column and convert to a common unit.

All Barley – Crop sorts alphabetically first, so the display starts with Barley’s own best yields (RM 380 in 2025 at 122 bu/ac on top).

title: Module 2 — Test Bank
text:
Questions 71–80 · Manitoba Wheat Variety
These questions use the full mb_wheat_varieties.csv – including the suppressed rows, where Reported is FALSE and the numeric columns are missing. Read it into an object called mb at the start of this block.

Question 71
(a) Filter mb to the reported rows (Reported == TRUE), saving as mb_rep. How many rows are in the filtered data frame?
(b) From mb_rep, select Municipality, Variety, and Yield_bu_ac, saving the result. Report its column names.
(c) In a comment: how many rows does mb itself still have, and what happened to the suppressed rows in mb_rep?


Answer

mb_rep <- filter(mb, Reported == TRUE)
nrow(mb_rep)
mb_slim <- select(mb_rep, Municipality, Variety, Yield_bu_ac)
names(mb_slim)


2,398 rows.


Municipality, Variety, Yield_bu_ac.


mb still has 5,358 rows – filtering returns a new data frame. The 2,960 suppressed rows are simply absent from mb_rep; they were not deleted from anything.





Question 72
(a) From mb_rep (reported rows), filter to the varieties AAC BRANDON (BW 932) or AAC STARBUCK <SECAN> using |, saving the result. How many rows are in the filtered data frame?
(b) Write the same filter using %in% and confirm the count matches.
(c) In a comment: a classmate wrote the condition with & instead of | and got zero rows. Why?


Answer

two_var <- filter(mb_rep, Variety == "AAC BRANDON (BW 932)" | Variety == "AAC STARBUCK <SECAN>")
nrow(two_var)
two_var2 <- filter(mb_rep, Variety %in% c("AAC BRANDON (BW 932)", "AAC STARBUCK <SECAN>"))
nrow(two_var2)

(a, b) 893 rows both ways.

& demands both conditions true of the same row, and no single row’s variety is both names at once. “Or” is the right connector.





Question 73
(a) Filter mb_rep to yields above 80 bu/ac, saving the result. How many rows are in the filtered data frame?
(b) Filter that result again to 2024 only. How many rows now?
(c) Sort your over-80 data frame from (a) best-first. Which municipality, variety, and year top the list, at what yield?


Answer

high <- filter(mb_rep, Yield_bu_ac > 80)
nrow(high)
high_2024 <- filter(high, Year == 2024)
nrow(high_2024)
arrange(high, desc(Yield_bu_ac))


97 rows. (b) 16 rows.


HILLSBURG-ROBLIN-SHELL RIVER, BOLLES <SEED DEPOT>, in 2022, at 97.8 bu/ac.





Question 74
(a) From mb_rep, make a version with only Year, Municipality, Variety, and Yield_bu_ac – once by naming what you keep, once by dropping what you don’t (Farms, Acres, Reported) – saving each, and confirm the two have the same column names. Then make a third version keeping the adjacent range Year:Variety and report its names.
(b) Rename Yield_bu_ac to yield, saving the result, and show the new column names.


Answer

kept    <- select(mb_rep, Year, Municipality, Variety, Yield_bu_ac)
dropped <- select(mb_rep, -Farms, -Acres, -Reported)
names(kept)
names(dropped)
ranged  <- select(mb_rep, Year:Variety)
names(ranged)
renamed <- rename(mb_rep, yield = Yield_bu_ac)
names(renamed)


Identical four names both ways; the range version keeps Year, Municipality, Variety.


The same seven columns with yield in place of Yield_bu_ac.





Question 75
(a) From mb_rep, use one mutate() to add total_bu, each observation’s acres times its yield, saving the result.
(b) Compute the mean of total_bu.
(c) Sort by total_bu, largest first. Which municipality tops the table, and at roughly what total?
(d) In a comment: what does total_bu measure that Yield_bu_ac does not?


Answer

mb_rep <- mutate(mb_rep, total_bu = Acres * Yield_bu_ac)
mean(mb_rep$total_bu)
arrange(mb_rep, desc(total_bu))


Mean 382,865 bu.


PORTAGE LA PRAIRIE, at about 5.13 million bushels.


Production – how much grain the planting actually produced – rather than how well each acre yielded. A modest yield on enormous acres can out-produce a great yield on few.





Question 76
A bushel of wheat is 60 lb, so one bu/ac is about 0.0673 t/ha.
(a) Filter mb_rep to 2025, saving the result. How many rows are in the filtered data frame?
(b) Add a yield_t_ha column with mutate(), saving the result, and compute its mean.
(c) In a comment: the canola conversion factor in the chapters was 0.0560. Why is wheat’s different?


Answer

rep_2025 <- filter(mb_rep, Year == 2025)
nrow(rep_2025)
rep_2025 <- mutate(rep_2025, yield_t_ha = Yield_bu_ac * 0.0673)
mean(rep_2025$yield_t_ha)


438 rows.


Mean 4.58 t/ha.


A bushel is a volume standardized by weight per crop – wheat’s bushel is 60 lb and canola’s is 50 lb – so the bu/ac-to-t/ha factor differs crop by crop.





Question 77
(a) Sort mb_rep from highest yield to lowest, and report the municipality, variety, and year in the top row.
(b) Sort it from lowest to highest instead. What changes in the code?
(c) In a comment: after (a) and (b), is mb_rep itself now sorted? Why or why not?


Answer

arrange(mb_rep, desc(Yield_bu_ac))
arrange(mb_rep, Yield_bu_ac)


HILLSBURG-ROBLIN-SHELL RIVER, BOLLES <SEED DEPOT>, 2022, at 97.8 bu/ac.


Drop the desc().


No – neither sorted result was assigned; both were displayed and discarded.





Question 78
A script contains, in order:
filter(mb, Reported == FALSE)
suppressed <- filter(mb, Reported == FALSE)
(a) In a comment: what does each line do, and what appears in the console after each?
(b) Report nrow(suppressed) and nrow(mb).
(c) In a comment: the suppressed rows have no yields. What did MASC suppress them for, according to the dataset description?


Answer



Line 1 computes the suppressed rows and prints them, saving nothing. Line 2 computes the same thing and saves it as suppressed, printing nothing.


nrow(suppressed) is 2,960; nrow(mb) is still 5,358.


Too few farms grew that variety in that municipality – the value is withheld to protect individual farms’ privacy, not because it was never measured.





Question 79
(a) From mb_rep, filter to the municipality ALEXANDER, saving the result. How many rows are in the filtered data frame?
(b) Select Variety, Year, and Yield_bu_ac from it, saving again.
(c) Sort so the best observation is on top. Which variety was it, at what yield?


Answer

alexander <- filter(mb_rep, Municipality == "ALEXANDER")
nrow(alexander)
alexander <- select(alexander, Variety, Year, Yield_bu_ac)
arrange(alexander, desc(Yield_bu_ac))


17 rows.


AAC ELIE(BW931), at 90.9 bu/ac.





Question 80
(a) Using head(), display the first six rows of mb.
(b) Sort mb_rep by Acres in descending order into a new object, select its Municipality, Variety, Year, and Acres columns into another, and display the first six rows.
(c) In a comment: what does the top row of (b) tell you, and why did we sort mb_rep rather than mb?


Answer

head(mb)
by_acres <- arrange(mb_rep, desc(Acres))
big <- select(by_acres, Municipality, Variety, Year, Acres)
head(big)

(b, c) The biggest single planting is AAC BRANDON (BW 932) in PORTAGE LA PRAIRIE, 2020, at 74,604 acres. We sorted the reported rows because the suppressed rows have no acre values to sort on.

title: Module 2 — Test Bank
text:
Questions 81–90 · Canada Field Crops
These questions use the full statcan_field_crops.csv – thirteen crops by province, 2015–2025. Read it into an object called crops at the start of this block.

Question 81
(a) Filter crops to Saskatchewan, saving the result. How many rows are in the filtered data frame?
(b) From it, select Year, Crop, and Yield_bu_ac, saving the result, and report its column names.
(c) In a comment: how many rows does crops itself still have, and why?


Answer

sask <- filter(crops, Province == "Saskatchewan")
nrow(sask)
sask_slim <- select(sask, Year, Crop, Yield_bu_ac)
names(sask_slim)


137 rows.


Year, Crop, Yield_bu_ac.


Still 1,067 – the functions return new data frames and leave the original untouched.





Question 82
(a) Filter to the three prairie provinces – Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba – using %in%, saving the result. How many rows are in the filtered data frame?
(b) Write the same filter with two |s and confirm the count matches.
